EntertainmentTab.title: Celebrity Traitors star Michael Sheen says being an actor will be a 'disadvantage'
EntertainmentTab.text:
Michael Sheen has said he thinks being an actor will be a disadvantage while he is on Celebrity Traitors.

The 57-year-old is among the stars who will go head to head in the second series of the BBC reality game spin-off.

A total of 21 presenters, comedians, actors and musicians will try their hand at being traitors and faithfuls in the show, which airs on 1 October.

The Hollywood actor from Port Talbot said he wanted to participate because he is a "big fan" of the show and wanted to be in the castle after previously filming in the area.

Speaking about how his public persona may affect how others perceive and treat him on the show, the actor said: "Well, I do think it's a disadvantage to be an actor because people immediately go, 'oh well, he pretends for a living'.

"I don't think that is the case, because the whole point of acting is that you have to trick yourself into believing that what you're doing is true. If you are consciously aware that you're pretending or you're saying things that aren't true, then it's bad acting. It's just bad.

"Just for me being an actor, I think that's a disadvantage because people are already suspicious of that.

"Beyond being an actor, just my persona, I don't really know what people think about me. So, I don't know if it'll help or not."

Sheen portrayed the disgraced Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor in the 2024 Prime Video series, A Very Royal Scandal.

It was based on the 2019 BBC Newsnight interview conducted by Emily Maitlis with Mountbatten-Windsor regarding his relationship with Jeffrey Epstein, and became a defining moment in modern royal and media history.

Sheen has also starred in films including Frost/Nixon, The Damned United and The Special Relationship.

Sheen said: "I knew the area a bit [where Traitors is filmed in Scotland], and it is stunningly beautiful. It's a lovely place to be and the game is just fascinating.

"I think for a show to be so popular and to grab the cultural imagination so much, it has to have the ability to go beyond what its genre is.

"It somehow speaks to something a bit deeper, maybe. People get so absorbed in it."

EntertainmentTab.title: Somerset Booker Prize nominee praises former school teachers
EntertainmentTab.text:
An author whose latest book has been nominated for the prestigious Booker Prize said childhood boredom inspired his creativity.

Luke Kennard, who grew up in Chard in Somerset, has been shortlisted for Black Bag, which is based on an experiment involving an actor sitting in a bin bag at the back of a lecture hall.

He said, as a child, he had "quite a lot of time to practice" his creative passions.

Kennard also praised his teachers at the town's Holyrood Academy and said: "It just can't be exaggerated how much difference a teacher can make when they find a kid who has a passion for their subjects."

Kennard said growing up in a quiet town had an impact on his "creative impulse".

"You stay in your room playing the clarinet or writing a poem - there's a certain virtue to being a little bit bored sometimes, and just having to amuse yourself."

Kennard attended Holyrood Academy from 1992 to 1999 and studied both GCSE and A-level English Literature.

He added: "It was the teachers that I had who really encouraged my writing- that's quite foundational."

Kennard said the former head of English, Paul Coffman, would read his short stories during break times, and leave him notes and suggestions.

"He was the first person who really got me to take my writing seriously."

EntertainmentTab.title: Gisele Pelicot rape case play to be staged in central London
EntertainmentTab.text:
A play telling the "harrowing" story of the Gisele Pelicot rape case will be performed in London at a one-off event at London County Hall, on the South Bank.

Ms Pelicot's ex-husband, Dominique Pelicot, was jailed for 20 years for drugging and raping her, as well as allowing other men to rape her while she was unconscious, in abuse that lasted nearly a decade.

The 73-year-old, who waived her right to anonymity as a survivor of sexual abuse, said shame should fall on her abusers, not her.

Thirty actors and public figures will take part in the "documentary theatre" style performance, created from documents from the trial and psychiatric reports of the 51 men who were prosecuted.

The Pelicot Rape Trial created by Swiss director and playwright Milo Rau started as a stand-alone piece as part of the Festival d'Avignon, an arts festival in the town where the crimes took place.

The performance then travelled across cities in Europe, with only one show per location.

Milo Rau said: "It's about disentangling the story from the couple Gisèle and Dominique Pelicot – turning it into a story that belongs to all of us and at the same time to none of us."

In London, the piece is being put on at London County Hall, by the Young Vic Theatre, on 30 November.

The theatre's website said the performance is a "profoundly affecting piece of documentary theatre, comprised of testimonies and written accounts from the trial, (which) pays tribute to the ordinary woman who opened the way to change".

It added: "The Pelicot trial is undoubtedly the most publicised, discussed, and symbolic of our time.

"As a sociological study it shows that in a typical Western European city – the small town of Mazan in the south of France – perfectly ordinary men from all social classes and age groups are capable of perhaps the most extreme crime: the repeated rape of an unconscious woman."

Fifty men were found guilty of rape or sexual offences after a three-and-a-half-month trial.

Young Vic Theatre's artistic director and chief executive, Nadia Fall said: "Milo Rau's extraordinary testimonial piece The Pelicot Trial breaks out beyond our theatre walls to County Hall; a piece of confronting event-theatre which bears witness to the harrowing story of Gisèle Pelicot."

EntertainmentTab.title: Slipknot reveal world tour with Marilyn Manson as support act
EntertainmentTab.text:
Heavy metal band Slipknot have announced a new world tour, with Marilyn Manson due to appear as a support act.

The eight-piece group, known for performing in masks, will be joined by the US rock musician during their shows at London's Wembley Stadium and multiple dates of the South American leg of the tour.

Some fans have reacted angrily to the news and said they will not attend the shows over past sexual abuse accusations against the 57-year-old.

Manson, real name Brian Warner, has always strongly denied any allegations against him.

Thousands of fans replied to an Instagram post featuring the line-up for the London gigs, which also includes metalcore band Hatebreed.

While some posts expressed excitement at the support acts, many were critical of Manson's presence on the bill, describing it as "disappointing".

Others, who described themselves as long-time Slipknot fans, said they would not buy tickets for the show in protest at his appearance.

One wrote: "Would've loved to see this but there's literally nothing you could do to get my cash in Manson's pockets."

Another added the announcement was "such a disappointment" and they would not be attending.

However, others disagreed, with one pointing out the two acts have a "huge fanbase overlap" and describing Manson as a "perfect support act".

EntertainmentTab.title: Sir Ranulph Fiennes' relatives tell BBC it's 'very painful' not being able to visit him
EntertainmentTab.text:
Relatives of the British explorer Sir Ranulph Fiennes have said it is "very painful" he appears to have been hidden away from them.

Speaking to BBC Newsnight, his sister-in-law told the BBC that she did not know where he was, and nobody had been able to see him.

It has been alleged that Sir Ranulph, 82, has been admitted to a number of care homes under assumed names, after a family rift involving his second wife, Louise Millington-Cotes.

Louise Millington-Cotes did not immediately respond to the allegations, or the BBC's request for comment.

Cheshire Police have said they are aware of the concerns regarding Sir Ranulph, and are satisfied he is living in an appropriate setting with suitable care.

They said there were "no immediate safeguarding concerns".

Sir Ranulph has not been seen in public for nearly two years, just months after opening up about a diagnosis of Parkinson's disease, a progressive disorder affecting the brain, nervous system, and muscle control.

He was the first person to visit both north and south poles by surface means in the early 1980s and has been described by Guinness World Records as "the world's greatest living explorer".

Spending his childhood between the UK and South Africa, he joined the British Army after leaving school, going on to serve in the SAS.

Sir Ranulph's stepson, Alex Millington-Cotes, told BBC Newsnight he wanted to see the power of attorney "removed from my own mother" and placed in the hands of people who "have fully his best interests in mind".

"He's not an isolated type of person, and so to see him isolated now is very painful," he said.

Last week, he launched a crowdfunding campaign for legal fees to "locate and safeguard" the explorer, and so far it has raised almost £26,000.

He wrote that the fundraiser had been created as "a result of our concern and desperation" after trying "multiple avenues" to locate his stepfather.

Questions about Sir Ranulph's whereabouts grew in prominence after a report in the Telegraph earlier this month, external in which "members of his inner circle" raised concerns about his whereabouts.

The paper also reported concerns about Sir Ranulph have been raised with the Office of the Public Guardian (OPG), the government agency which helps people to stay in control of decisions about their health and finances.

In a statement to the BBC, an OPG spokesperson said: "We have a strict duty of confidentiality to all individuals who have made a lasting power of attorney, and it would be deeply inappropriate to comment on a specific case.

"We take all safeguarding concerns seriously and investigate thoroughly where there is the evidence and legal basis to do so."

EntertainmentTab.title: MTV VMAs: Taylor Swift breaks record as Madonna also wins
EntertainmentTab.text:
Taylor Swift took home the video of the year award as she became the most successful artist in the history of the MTV Video Music Awards on Sunday.

The singer went into the night tied with Beyoncé on 30 wins, and went on to score the night's top award for the visuals for her track The Fate of Ophelia, taken from her 2025 album The Life of a Showgirl.

The original Queen of Pop, Madonna, won artist of the year, best dance and best collaboration alongside Sabrina Carpenter for their dancefloor-filler Bring Your Love, which was the lead single from Madonna's 2026 album Confessions II.

Swift also received the inaugural award for artist director, having written and directed the 1990s infomercial parody video for another song, Opalite.

She dedicated her new award to the "ultimate showgirl", saying: "I think we were all very lucky to share this planet with Dolly Parton for a time".

The 36-year-old also debuted the music video for her new song Patient Zero - starring actors Colin Farrell and Dakota Johnson - during the Los Angeles ceremony, hosted by rapper Snoop Dogg.

The dark gothic thriller is her first music video since marrying NFL player Travis Kelce.

The song is one of four new tracks on The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore, which dropped last week.

In a ceremony that largely awarded female artists, Madonna went into the night with the most nominations - 13.

And her team also won best cinematography and choreography both for Confessions II, the film.

"Most of you were probably not born when I performed at the very first VMAs 43 years ago," the 68-year-old said after winning artist of the year.

She went on to recall how she had fallen over and exposed her backside, an accident which had threatened to end her fledgling career.

Reflecting on more recent times, she added: "I spent the last year and a half finding myself, believing in myself and really making the music that I wanted to make."

Madonna's opening performance - her first VMAs show since her infamous onstage kiss with Britney Spears in 2003 - included a live duet with Carpenter, and an appearance from British Brat star Charli XCX who features on her recent remix Danceteria (Afterhours).

While accepting the award for best collab, Madonna claimed Carpenter's team had originally kept her waiting.

"When five days passed and I still didn't get connected with Sabrina and didn't hear back from her about whether she wanted to do a song with me - five days - I DM'd [direct messaged] her," said the star.

"She answered me back and... within weeks we were in the studio together," she continued. "It was fabulous."

Carpenter, who grimaced slightly at the thought of her team having left the pop icon hanging, clarified: "My team replies. Just so everybody knows, they do respond to people.

"But I respond faster. So direct line to me is always the best way to get in contact."

British singers Raye and Sienna Spiro, who won best new artist, also performed on the night, where there were tributes to the late Parton and George Michael.

Another Brit, PinkPantheress won best art direction alongside Sweden's Zara Larsson for Stateside.

BTS picked up best group and song of the year for Swim, Olivia Rodrigo's The Cure won best alternative and Nirvana were honoured with the Video Vanguard award.

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘They’ll never bring us dowwwwwwwn!’ Wicked’s stars pick their favourite songs from the smash hit
EntertainmentTab.text:
Idina Menzel originated the role of Elphaba, the witch of the west who turns out not to be so wicked (but still very green). She won a Tony on Broadway, starred in the West End run and made a cheeky cameo in the recent film version

I’ll never forget the exhilaration I felt the first time I sang Defying Gravity in dress rehearsal. All the lights were as they should be. The smoke machine was blowing. The orchestra was playing. I was locked into my safety belt and I started to rise up over the theatre. To have that incredible moment and to see how the audience leapt to their feet – I felt so proud but I also just wanted to cry.

I was part of the developmental process of writing Wicked for four years and stood at a piano with [composer and lyricist] Stephen Schwartz many a time, being introduced to new ideas and songs – often written just the night before. He came to really understand my voice. Not just how high I could hit a note but where it sat emotionally. Originally, Defying Gravity didn’t go up an octave at the end. It stayed in this low place. So I asked Stephen if I could take it up an octave – the whole song is soaring, I said, and I have it in me to go up there: “Looook to the western skiiiiiiy!” I do take credit for that change.

The final note is actually easy for me. It’s like a release. There are other notes I find much harder. Singing notes on an “E” vowel is not easy: “Bring meeeee down”, that’s really tricky. I actually botched that note in my call-back audition. But instead of falling to pieces, I looked at the accompanist and said: “I’m going to do that again.” And then I just took all this angst and frustration at not being perfect and nailed it. Joe Mantello [director of Wicked on Broadway] always told me that’s how he knew I was going to be their witch – because I had this power and ferocity about me. That’s why, to this day, whenever young people ask me for advice, I always tell them not to fear their mistakes. Embrace those moments.

Zizi Strallen plays Glinda the Good in the current West End cast. She’s used to stepping into the shoes of iconic roles – and hinting at cracks that lie beneath a pristine surface – after a breakout performance as Mary Poppins

Whatever you’re going through in your life, Wicked somehow manages to hit a nerve. Everyone can relate to not feeling accepted for who they truly are or trying to figure out different parts of their personality. I’ve definitely gone through phases where I’ve made mistakes or said the wrong thing – so I channel all of that when I sing.

Thank Goodness shows the journey Glinda goes on throughout the whole show. It tells the audience that’s she’s struggling with the prospect of fame and recognition – and all the things that come with being Glinda the Good – but also wanting to stand up for her friend Elphaba and for what’s right. She’s getting everything she ever dreamed of but at what cost? That’s a beautiful arc for any actor to play: to start a song at one point and finish at an entirely different emotional one.

It’s wonderful to perform but very difficult to learn. The rhythms are really different to how you think they’re going to be. Stephen wrote it so that it’s sung exactly the way you would speak it, with little gaps here and there: “There’s a kind of a sort of – cost.” It’s similar to the way that Sondheim writes. It only really made sense to me when I sang it with the full orchestra and their rhythms accompanying me.

Dancing Through Life

Jordan Litz played Fiyero, the student who gets romantically entangled with Glinda and Elphaba, more than 1,700 times in the US. He makes his West End debut in the role

Dancing Through Life wasn’t always in the show. It was originally a song called Which Way Is the Party? The lyrics were a little sleazy: “Which way is the next keg of winkie beer?” It was all very frat boy and didn’t have nearly the same carefree attitude. You can hear they kept some stuff from the original number – the intro and the bridge – but the rest of the song is much more light and easy.

This was initially the hardest song for me to do because it’s the one that’s least like me. Growing up, I wasn’t the super-cool popular kid. I was 5ft 4in in my freshman year, singing soprano in my high-school choir and wearing oversized trainers. Finding the confidence to play Fiyero didn’t come naturally. It was always the song I got the most notes on during rehearsals for the Broadway run. More swagger! More confidence!

For the first year, performing it was a constant battle – trying to find that carefree confidence. And that struggle would show up in my dancing. My moves weren’t big enough or sharp enough. You’re surrounded by these incredible dancers and it’s very easy to shrink into yourself and not commit. It took a lot of support from people around me, convincing me that I have it inside myself. I was fighting against the person I envisioned myself to be, growing up, and who I actually am today. That’s probably why it’s become my favourite number: it feels like the song that I’ve learned the most from.

Musical supervisor Stephen Oremus conducted and helped to craft the Broadway premiere of Wicked

The Wizard and I was Stephen’s third try at a song in that spot in the show and it unlocked Elphaba’s journey. The first try felt very earnest and wide-eyed. It was a beautiful and heartfelt song called Making Good, about this young green girl who just wanted to do good things. But it wasn’t quite multi-layered enough. The second attempt was written after Idina was cast. It was a little bit more soaring and it suited Idina’s voice and personality more: it was the next step towards giving the number more of a sweeping grand gesture. Then in the third version, Stephen just hit it. He was able to combine everything good from the other takes and make it work. It’s an amazingly simple song but brilliantly written and executed.

The way we built the orchestrations, you can feel the excitement and anticipation of the character. The colours and flow of the song are relatively simple as Elphaba’s working out her thoughts and then it all shifts when she gets to that “unlimited” bridge. The orchestration gets dreamy and really expansive musically. Elphaba throws her arm out and allows herself to really feel for the first time. You’re seeing this very cerebral and intense girl start to get excited about the possibility of it all. It’s overwhelmingly beautiful to me.

The offers from Hollywood came flooding in after Gregory Maguire wrote his novel Wicked, a spin on L Frank Baum’s The Wizard of Oz. But it wasn’t until composer and lyricist Stephen Schwartz suggested setting it to song that an adaptation felt possible – and Wicked’s musical journey began

The final song between Elphaba and Glinda was one that I approached very cautiously. I knew it was going to be the heart of the show. If we got it right, we had our emotional ending. If we didn’t, it could undercut everything that had come before. So I phoned my collaborator, Winnie Holzman, and talked to her about this final meeting. What kind of things would they say to one another? At one point Winnie said: “They’ve had such an enormous impact on each other – they’ve changed each other for good.” “Stop right there,” I said. “You’ve just given me the title.”

I always knew what the song was going to feel like. I wanted something that was heartfelt and uncovered. Completely vulnerable. A lot of Glinda’s songs are about presenting a specific version of herself to the public. But I wanted this song to feel like a true expression from the heart. Then I started to think about the lyrics. My daughter Jessica was visiting at the time. She’d always had a deep friendship with a woman, Sarah, whom she first met when they were six or seven. So I sat down with Jess and I said: “Imagine you’re only going to see Sarah one last time. What would you say?” Jess started to talk about people coming into each other’s lives for a reason, about helping and hurting each other and about forgiveness. I wrote it all down and that was pretty much the entire first verse of For Good. I think that’s one of the reasons the song has such an impact – because people intuitively feel the truth of it.

EntertainmentTab.title: Digger review – Tom Cruise’s loudmouth oil tycoon goes hard in Alejandro G Iñárritu’s eco-satire
EntertainmentTab.text:
A new movie from the Oscar-winning Mexican director Alejandro González Iñárritu is always an event. So it’s disconcerting to discover that the event in question is the most disappointing film of the year: an exasperatingly shallow, laborious, self-congratulatory satire with a trick up its sleeve, featuring very good actors giving not very good performances. There are moments to enjoy in Tom Cruise’s boisterous leading turn, yes, but the film’s value resides chiefly in some dreamlike and disturbing images, distorted and bulging from the screen, conjured by cinematographer Emmanuel Lubezki and production designer Dennis Gassner.

An ageing, paunchy Texan oil tycoon called “Digger” Rockwell is seen fretfully getting up in the morning, cooing over his horrible old incontinent cat, taking urgent messages from underlings about a certain situation developing in his drilling station in the frozen Arctic. He is played by Tom Cruise with a wispy baldingness and various other prostheses, together with a good-ol’-boy twang and a Stetson borrowed from Slim Pickens’s bomb-riding army major in Kubrick’s Dr Strangelove. His prized possession is the battered old shovel his granddaddy used a century before, digging for black gold as a penniless young man in the lone star state. Digger likes to brandish this to make a point.

Digger’s – and the world’s – troubles come to a head when he is informed by his cringingly polite, querulous and terrified chief scientist Ganesh (Riz Ahmed) that the company’s irresponsible drilling practices, of which Ganesh has been warning Digger for quite some time, have caused a crisis: a vast ice floe, many times the size of Manhattan island, has broken away from the Arctic landmass and is now moving quickly towards the coast of Norway. Its imminent landfall is going to be like a nuclear attack.

Aggressively unrepentant to the very end, Digger gets himself invited to the White House’s crisis meeting, chaired by the gaunt and unwell President Compson, crankily played by John Goodman, with various military top brass and besuited politicians, including the vice-president, a very bland role on which Michael Stuhlbarg is wasted. Digger effectively takes over as de facto C-in-C, lambasting the president’s pusillanimous reluctance to take responsibility for a situation that his political subsidies and permissions have created. Meanwhile, back at Digger’s residence, Sandra Hüller has next to nothing to do as his half-sister, a role whose substance may well have been abandoned in the edit.

But wait. The film’s shrill, scratchy characterisations are partly explained by a sudden, unexpected plot development, yet this only creates a second narrative strand in which the performances are … well … merely inhibited and uninteresting. Cruise’s set piece moment is his toweringly contemptuous speech to a stylised megaparliament of UN nincompoops, all of them shouting and pointing and dressed in grey, in which Digger defiantly lacerates their hypocrisy in affecting to despise oil, while remaining utterly addicted to it for all their consumer conveniences. (Tactfully, Digger does not attack movie stars’ private planes.) He also angrily says that moving over to renewables, including nuclear, is simply not viable. Really? Yet Digger’s claim remains unchallenged, part of what we are perhaps supposed to admire, in spite of ourselves, about his realist sense of everyone else’s bad faith.

It is only when the film’s big storytelling sideways lurch happens, that you can see how our investment in the action is undermined; it is enclosed within inverted commas, an unearned and somehow anticlimactic high concept, a situation which is not itself fully dramatised or investigated but presented as a fait accompli twist. As with Adam McKay’s Don’t Look Up, there may be a tacit consensus, understandable at some level, that at least we have a big mainstream movie which is talking about the biggest issue of our time, and we have a duty to suspend critical objection. Digger certainly resonates with Donald Trump’s greedy urge to despoil the Arctic and everywhere else. Yet there is something glib and overblown here. This film finds itself in a postmodern hole. And what do you do when you’re in a hole?

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘Stern, sensuous, almost kissable lips’: why sculptures can have far more power when they’re broken
EntertainmentTab.text:
The nose of Cleopatra VII was supposed to have been so beautiful that it changed the course of history: if it had been shorter, French philosopher Blaise Pascal wrote, “the whole face of the earth would have changed”. A visit to the Palazzo Strozzi in Florence, however, will leave you convinced that Cleo’s conk was only the second most stunning feature to ever grace the face of an Egyptian pharaoh. Among the more than 80 objects on display at an exhibition that opened last week is an astonishingly lifelike sculpture showing off the lips of Akhenaten, from the 14th century BC: a seagull shape resting on a pillow of lush flesh, at once both stern and sensuous, almost uncomfortably kissable.

It was Thomas Aquinas who first came up with the theory that we perceive things to be beautiful when they are intact and whole, but the Akhenaten sculpture is so striking precisely because it has a major blemish. Like all the objects shown in Florence, it is only a fragment: a shard of polished limestone found in the dumps south of the Great Aten Temple in the city of el-Amarna, showing only the ruler’s nose and mouth.

“One of the unique qualities of fragments is that they focus your attention on details,” says CD Dickerson, an expert in Renaissance and baroque art. “You wouldn’t have considered the subtle way that the lip has been crisply carved in this stone if it had been part of a bigger statue with a bunch of other features. Fragments make you think about objects in a different way.”

Entitled Broken: The Power of Fragments, the show that Dickerson has co-curated for the Palazzo Strozzi and the National Gallery of Art in Washington DC, explores why people throughout history have gone to great lengths to damage or destroy carefully crafted sculptures and statues. But along the way, it raises an even more intriguing question: why it is that some works of art have a more powerful emotional pull in a broken state than when whole?

Many of the objects shown here speak of fault lines in history. There is a decapitated lifesize statue of a kneeling prior from Romainmôtier in Switzerland, likely beheaded during the iconoclastic frenzy of the Protestant Reformation. The dismembered left foot and right hand of King Louis XIV are all that remains of an equestrian monument to the French royal after the revolution rolled across Paris’s Place Vendôme and put up a guillotine instead. Modernist sculptor Adolfo Wildt’s bust of Mussolini was adorned with a simple bullet through the forehead after the fall of the fascist regime.

The vandals were following an age-old tradition, says co-curator Andrew Sears. “Across the ancient world it was a common practice during regime changes or religious transformations to destroy images of the previous one because it was believed that the images contained some kind of life force of the ruler.”

In some cases, these defaced sculptures would stay on as a deterrent. “They were made to be displayed in that way,” says Sears. A 19AD bust representing Germanicus, heir to Tiberius, had its nose expertly hacked off, upper earlobes cut and forehead adorned with a cross by Christians who protested against the deification of Roman emperors. The past, we are reassured, was a foreign country with cruel rituals.

Broken starts to get more surprising and interesting where it explores brokenness as more than a result of historical fractures. A section called Sculpting the Fragment opens with an intriguing dogū figurine from ancient Japan. Little is known about these small, fired-clay statuettes with bulging coffee-bean eyes other than that they have been found in pieces all over burial sites in Japan.

Current research indicates that the function of dogū figurines may have been akin to modern-day birthday pinatas: smashed to celebrate not just the end of the old but also the start of the new. “It’s very clear that the culture was to make these sculptures to intentionally break them, and for communities to share pieces with each other,” says Dickerson. “Our contemporary perception of ancient cultures being more violent is not always accurate.”

Dickerson and Sears’ rummage through the darker corners of museum storage rooms has yielded little evidence of Aquinas’s equation of breakage with ugliness. Often, the opposite held true. From the early 15th-century Aztec capital of Tenochtitlan, they present a statue of a reclining figure that was intentionally decapitated, as part of a campaign to rebuild a temple. Modelling their approach on the ruinous state of their surroundings, the Mexica seem to have understood completion to be unattainable. A broken artwork was proper because it revealed the true state of the world.

We may think of the cult of ruined buildings and broken statues as an obsession of the Romantics, of the paintings of Caspar David Friedrich or the “colossal wreck” of Percy Shelley’s Ozymandias. But Dickerson says ruin lust was already embedded in the art and literature of the Renaissance from the 13th century onwards. One of the most striking displays in Florence is a Michelangelo terracotta model of a headless and armless woman. Dated around 1533, it looks damaged but isn’t. Instead, it was the Renaissance’s answer to a pair of pre-distressed grunge-wash jeans: recent technical analysis of the torso’s breakage points suggests Michelangelo deliberately sculpted a fragment, in homage to the awe-inspiring antiquities that were being excavated in Rome at the time.

The exhibition culminates with contemporary artistic takes on broken sculptures, such as a Louise Bourgeois foot in a leg brace and German artist Julius von Bismarck’s collapsable equestrian statue of his chancellor forebear, Otto. If that feels slightly self-restraining, it’s because the wholeness v brokenness divide is still everywhere in modern popular culture once you start looking for it. Here the far-right social media accounts with immaculate classical busts as avatars, the impeccably smooth aesthetics of the iPhone, the flattened masks of the “clean girl” makeup trend; there the rise of broken bodies on the big screen, from Mad Max’s one-armed Furiosa to cleft-lipped lead actors like Tom Burke and Franz Rogowski and Game of Thrones’ “cripples, bastards and broken things”.

Clearly, the answer to the question of whether there is a beauty in brokenness is not just one that captured ancient civilisations, but continues to be one of the central cultural dividing lines of our time.

Broken: The Power of the Fragment is at Palazzo Strozzi, Florence, 25 September 2026 until 24 January, and at the National Gallery of Art, Washington, from 13 March to 27 June 2027

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘We wanted it to be a battlecry’: how Republica made 90s anthem Ready to Go
EntertainmentTab.text:
Saffron Sprackling, vocals

We always had a vision of mixing acid house with indie rock, and we managed to rent a space and build our own studio in London’s Shoreditch area, long before it got trendy. I had a little vocal booth called Hattie Jacques, in honour of the Carry On films but also because it’s Cockney rhyming slang [for shakes]. We spent all our money rewiring it, and that’s where we wrote, recorded and produced Ready to Go – 100 mixes later!

We were perfectionists and wanted to do it all ourselves. Every sonic element had to be special up to the point where we ended up arguing. Like at a rave when you stand and dance by the speakers, everything was done with the listener in mind.

It was a collaborative effort, but Johnny Male and I wrote most of the song’s lyrics and the melody. We had a really good camaraderie, finishing each other’s sentences, him on an acoustic guitar and me scribbling things down. Tim Dorney and Andy Todd worked more on the technology and synth sounds. We pooled our skills, resources and dreams.

The song is all about daily life and things that happened to us. We didn’t write anything too existential – I don’t really like singing about myself – but I’ve always believed in language and the power of the pen. I think it was Johnny who came up with the line, “Ready to go.” It had an anthemic feel and we wanted it to be a bit of a battlecry: “It’s a crack, I’m back!” That line was inspired by the Irish slang, craic. Writing lyrics and big choruses over electronic beats was one of the most difficult things because of the BPM, but I’ve always had a sort of punky voice that suits it.

It was as much about the delivery as it was the words. My personality was becoming feistier and I think the song came from that, but also it’s about being positive, making good out of bad, and coming together as one. That’s what the vibe is like in the acid-house scene.

It was an exciting time. Zeke Manyika, who was the drummer in Orange Juice, lived across the way and I used to shimmy across the roof and go down a ladder where he and his wife would make me sandwiches. Every Tuesday night we would go to Matt Johnson’s house [from the The] to play table football with Paul Webb from Talk Talk. Me being a lot younger, I was like, “Oh my God, these are my idols!” They treated me with respect and it really gave me a sense of confidence. And I got quite good at table football.

One day, a girl at my hairdressers said to me: “Saff, do you fancy being dangerous?” I went “All right then,” and they dyed my hair blood red like a London bus. Jarvis Cocker always said: “If you’ve got a hook and a great hairdo, you’ll be a pop star.” Visually, it really helped us, and people seemed to like it.

At the time it was hard to get gigs as a girl: it was important to be in one of the few female-led bands. There are some fantastic female artists today, but I still wish we had more women in bands. Last year Olivia Rodrigo invited me backstage because she had been singing Ready to Go on her world tour – such a lovely lady and so talented. She said that Republica were one of her favourite bands and that growing up she had a poster of me because she’s of Asian heritage, too. I gave her a big hug.

When Sunderland beat Chelsea in the Premier League in May 2026, the whole stadium was singing Ready to Go and it brought a tear to my eye. I was asked to sing on the pitch at the 2022 Fifa World Cup – I turned around and Lionel Messi was standing there.

Johnny Male, guitar

We had some good songs but we hadn’t had a hit yet. I remember the day Saff came in the studio with red hair. I said: “We’re gonna be massive!” It was the missing link.

Ready to Go’s music came first. Toddy found these great chords which became the chorus. They were simple but effective, so we thought we’d better write a verse.

We sampled all the guitars into an Akai S1000 out of necessity, as in those days we were using an Atari ST computer which only had MIDI. The vocals were recorded on an 8-track digital recorder. Computer music was still in its infancy, we were learning as we went along. Any money we earned from gigs was spent on studio equipment and outboard gear.

Lyrically, we were trying to talk about the things surrounding us at the time. Going out and staying up late, witnessing the world in the middle of the night, then reporting back. We tried to create something that incorporated all the things we loved about the house scene in a song with an alternative edge.

Touring America, we started to get picked up on MTV and we noticed it in the hotels at night. It was on heavy rotation and you could see by the crowds that the monster was unleashed. It was fantastic, but we still wanted to be on Top of the Pops. Then we came back and it all happened in the UK and Europe. There was a lot of goodwill behind us and we often said that with a title like Ready to Go you could probably sell anything.

I’m always slightly disappointed that on one of the last vocal takes, the line was: “Went home, stayed in bed all day / In your T-shirt”, which I thought was really good, but because I wasn’t concentrating as I should have been, the other line – “Your T-shirt’s dish dirt” – got in.

The funny thing about playing the song live is that it always feels like it’s building towards the next bit, even when it drops down. Especially when an audience is responding to it. It’s a trick I wish I could do every time I write a song, but there’s a kind of magic alchemy that somehow appears then vanishes again.

GeneralTab.title: One of the five men arrested near RAF Fairford called 999 himself
GeneralTab.text:
One of five men arrested near RAF Fairford in the early hours of Sunday morning had dialled 999 himself, the BBC understands.

The suspect called the police at 00:45 BST, almost an hour before a female farmer also dialled 999 after seeing men in balaclavas.

The five were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later terrorism offences after three vans were spotted, sparking a major security incident around the Gloucestershire base which the US military operates.

They were released on bail on Monday in what police described as an "investigative decision" "grounded in experience and strategy".

Police say a quantity of petrol but no explosive devices were found during searches of the vans.

Police were alerted to "three suspicious vehicles" in Whelford, a village which lies directly east of the base, by the farmer.

She told the BBC it was "pure luck" she had spotted them, having arrived home to find the road blocked and a "large group of hooded and masked men".

"I believe that my 999 call foiled whatever plans they had," she said.

A bomb disposal team arrived on scene shortly afterwards and a 400m (1,312ft) cordon was put in place.

But Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, told reporters on Tuesday that the police response that morning had been due to "a range of information".

Police cordons near the base are expected to be completely lifted on Wednesday, while residents from the 85 homes evacuated on Sunday have been allowed to return to their properties.

The five men are all UK nationals aged between 23 and 25. Four of them live in Westminster and one in Camden, and searches of their homes are now complete.

Taylor previously said their bail was "subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others" as they remained under investigation.

"The safety of the public is at the forefront of our investigative decision-making, and this was certainly the case yesterday," he said on Tuesday.

"I understand why this development was surprising to some, but I would like to reiterate that this is an investigative decision and one which is grounded in experience and strategy."

The RAF base has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force for decades.

In recent months, US bombers have taken off from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.

US President Donald Trump on Tuesday told journalists he was "disappointed" the five men had been released on bail.

GeneralTab.title: How did the RAF Fairford incident go from 'suspected bomb plot' to police bail?
GeneralTab.text:
On Sunday morning, the world was watching as drama unfolded in the village of Whelford.

Before sunrise, residents were called from their beds and told to evacuate as a huge police operation unfolded in the village, which is next door to RAF Fairford, a base used by the US Air Force.

One villager managed to take a picture of five men sitting on the ground, stripped to the waist, handcuffed and under armed guard.

They were arrested for offences under the Explosives Act. But now counter-terrorism detectives say no explosives were found in their three vans, only an "accelerant" - petrol.

What some newspapers called a "suspected bomb plot" ended in the suspects being bailed. So what was going on?

The US President Donald Trump asserted that the men had been trying to do "big damage" to the base. "We had them under view for a long time, and we got them," he declared.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said: "What could have happened in the UK over the weekend is a very serious situation. It's one that clearly involved the hands of a foreign actor."

But in a veiled criticism of that, the head Counter Terrorism Policing in the UK Laurence Taylor said that the worry that a lot of people had been experiencing had been "heightened by the international commentary".

He also defended his detectives' decision to give the suspects police bail with "very strict conditions". This had been criticised by President Trump.

Taylor said it was an "investigative decision and one which is grounded in experience and strategy".

This suggests there were good tactical reasons for releasing the men on bail, perhaps to encourage their cooperation.

In truth, once it became clear that the military remote-controlled robots that were used found no explosives in the vans, only petrol, the investigation inevitably changed.

It left detectives with five men from London in their 20s in police custody who had simply been found parked up near the air base in the middle of the night in suspicious circumstances and with some petrol - but little other usable concrete evidence.

It might have been hard to persuade a senior officer or a magistrate to extend the suspects' detention without something more definite.

The men were being held under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act (PACE), not the Terrorism Act (TACT). This meant detectives had the option to use police bail with strict conditions, but could not hold the men for 14 days, which they could have done if TACT had been used.

For a while it was unclear whether the men were already being watched by undercover surveillance teams when they were spotted by villagers in the dead of night, or whether the villagers really were the first people to alert the police.

Taylor has now given some assistance on this, saying the response on Sunday morning was "due to a range of information that we received", suggesting the police had some other intelligence

Certainly security had been visibly stepped up at the base in the preceding days, so certainly there had been some intelligence about a possible attack. Elite firearms officers were very quick to respond to the villagers' 999 calls.

Both counter-terrorism and military sources have told me that this story is still quite near the beginning, raising the possibility that detectives are trying to identify some kind of "controlling hand" behind the presence of the suspects in Whelford with their petrol.

That leaves a number of options open:

The men could be entirely innocent and able to give a good explanation for being in Whelford on Sunday

They could have been paid or tricked into moving the vehicles and the petrol, but unaware of who they were working for

Or they could have been part of a plot which was interrupted before it reached a more dangerous phase

That is why the next bit of the counter-terrorism investigation is so vital.

By examining mobile phones and computers, tracking vehicles, searching addresses, and using the covert techniques of MI5, GCHQ and US intelligence, detectives are trying to build a clearer picture.

On that critical investigation rests the decision over whether to arrest anyone else, whether to charge the five men, and whether we ever find out the true story of the mysterious RAF Fairford plot.

GeneralTab.title: Household energy bills forecast to see biggest rise in four years
GeneralTab.text:
Household energy prices are set to soar in January, with a typical annual bill forecast to jump by £276, figures shared with the BBC reveal.

The 16% predicted increase would hit millions of households at the coldest time of year, and would mark the biggest rise in bills for four years.

The forecast from consultancy Cornwall Insight comes a day before prices go up under regulator Ofgem's October price cap and puts increased pressure on the government to support those who will struggle to pay.

Meanwhile, the boss of supplier EDF Simone Rossi has warned the UK is "walking into a second energy crisis" and called for an extension to the VAT cut on electricity which kicks in on Thursday.

About 20 million households in England, Scotland and Wales are on variable energy tariffs set by Ofgem's price cap, which puts a maximum price on each unit of gas and electricity.

Those homes will see a 4% increase in prices on Thursday, the equivalent of about £60 per year – or £5 per month – taking an annual bill to £1,723 for the typical household using both electricity and gas and paying by direct debit if this level was sustained for a year.

That rise would have been higher without the government's VAT cut, which knocks the equivalent of about £45 a year off a typical bill.

But forecasts show a far greater increase is possible for bills in January. Cornwall Insight said its latest forecast suggests the typical annual bill would rise to £1,999.

The forecast 16% rise will come at the worst time of year, according to Craig Lowrey, principal consultant at Cornwall Insight.

"These prices are going to hit households hard. January is already a difficult month for many, with cold weather and bank balances still recovering from Christmas," he said.

The predicted rise is the result of disruption of gas supplies owing to the conflict in the Middle East, and the resulting low gas storage levels in Europe. Rebuilding those stocks could mean high bills "well beyond the winter", the forecaster said.

Cornwall Insight has a strong track record on forecasts and is widely respected across the industry and politics. Similar forecasts have been made by energy suppliers.

This remains only a prediction at this stage. Ofgem will not announce the actual January price change until late November.

While an easing of tensions in the Middle East could lessen the pain for billpayers, the price setting period for the January cap is already halfway through.

With little sign of a truce or lower international energy costs, a big increase in prices for those not on a fixed tariff looks highly likely. Lowrey said a January rise was "all but certain".

That will be tough for people like Aaron Richards from Maidenhead.

"I try to eat less takeaways, work more overtime, and try to budget a bit better, but at the same time, we shouldn't have to," he said.

Aaron drives a diesel car, and so is paying record high prices to travel to and from work.

"I just feel like everything's going up. How far is it going to go? Someone's got to step in," he said.

"I know people who can't afford to heat their house and they're struggling at the moment. Housing and eating are two of life's essentials that everyone should have. It shouldn't be a challenge to have any of those things."

Among others calling for government help for struggling billpayers is Simone Rossi, chief executive of supplier EDF Energy.

Speaking exclusively to the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast, Mr Rossi said: "We are actually walking into a second significant energy crisis after the one we experienced just four years ago."

He said that the government should extend the cut in VAT on electricity bills from 5% to 0% beyond April, when it is due to expire.

He also urged ministers to give the go-ahead to the new Jackdaw gas field off the coast of Aberdeen, and the Rosebank oil field off Shetland.

The government has consistently said that it will consider ways to offer breathing space to billpayers on the cost of living.

Additional reporting by Oliver Smith and Paul Seddon. Graphics by Miguel Roca-Terry.

GeneralTab.title: Triple lock move is significant, but it's a gamble
GeneralTab.text:
It was a significant announcement from Prime Minister Andy Burnham on his plans for the triple lock after the general election. It will reverberate well beyond the hall.

For months, I have heard suggestions that Andy Burnham was warm to the idea that the triple lock as we know it had to go.

I had expected him to try to forge a political consensus on this thorny issue at this stage, but he has gone further than that. He has tried to take the sting out of the politics of his decision by tying it to funding a new national social care service.

The government calls it an "adjusted triple lock" as it is keen that pensioners are reassured. It is more like a double lock plus. The sensitivity over this political gamble is clear.

Under Burnham's plans, the state pension will go up by either the pace of price rises or 2.5%, whichever is higher. So, it will still keep up with inflation and go up every year.

The link to rises in yearly average earnings, which is the factor currently setting the rise under the triple lock, will be gone on an annual basis and instead be reflected over time.

The policy would be to maintain the state pension as a share of earnings at the record level it is due to reach in 2030.

This change is sharper than expected. Not a review or a consultation. Ministers and MPs will have to back the plans in interviews and, at some point, MPs will have to vote on changing the historic annual earnings link to the state pension.

It seems far more significant than a mere "adjustment". This will save many billions in the coming decades, but not so much in the next few years.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies thinktank says that, had Burnham's tweak been in place since 2011, it would have more than halved the annual £16bn cost of the triple lock, a £9bn saving every year. Government sources said the decision to make the change now will save around £15bn a year by 2040.

The prime minister was repeatedly advised that bond markets would show some appreciation for a UK government capable of taking tough decisions. Former chancellor Rachel Reeves might have imagined the same reward for her decision to scrap the winter fuel allowance, which was one of her first acts and later reversed.

Part of the UK premium in bond markets has been an understandable perception that UK politics cannot have long-term debates. And the triple lock is only one of the debates started by today's speech – with significant further moves on energy and post-Brexit policy expected – that the prime minister and chancellor need the markets as well as the country to get behind.

GeneralTab.title: Why female DIY is having a moment
GeneralTab.text:
It's hard to miss the explosion of DIY content that has hit our social media feeds over the last decade.

From quick reels on how to fix cracks in walls, to complicated YouTube tutorials on building alcove seating from scratch, the internet is chock-a-block with seemingly endless home improvement demos.

While DIY was once seen as more of a male domain, female influencers are inspiring a new generation of women to take matters into their own hands.

Meanwhile, demand for female professionals is rising, while some women are changing careers to take up trades which they see as more AI-proof than their desk jobs.

DIY influencer Jasmine Gurney has documented an impressive and exhausting sounding list of tasks on Instagram.

She has torn down partition walls, replaced flooring, erected a fence, insulated and boarded her loft, built an outdoor workshop, made custom cabinetry, moved plug sockets, made her son his first bed and has been building him a treehouse.

Eight months pregnant, the former marketer is now racing to finish building a fitted wardrobe before the new baby arrives.

"I like proving people wrong," says Jasmine, 33, from Bedfordshire, who says she's been trolled by people questioning her techniques but they just "spur me on more".

"I'm showing and empowering other women to do it," she says.

"I've shown me doing things whilst pregnant, I've had my firstborn strapped to me in a baby carrier while doing things.

"I'm just showing that we are capable, we are interested in this sort of stuff and... we're sick of waiting around for six months for our husbands to pick up the tools and do it in most cases."

Gen Z women are "leading the charge in challenging gendered DIY stereotypes", according to a 2024 report by B&Q.

Around three-quarters of Gen Z women surveyed said they enjoy DIY, compared to 60% of all female respondents.

And 82% of Gen Z women said seeing women doing more complex home DIY on social media had inspired them to do more themselves, versus 60% of women in general.

Of course, not all jobs are DIY. Sometimes you'll need to GSI (get someone in).

Bliss Cunneen walked away from an Anthropology university course in 2020 to train as a plumber.

The 28-year-old from south London says trying the trade on a whim is the "best thing I've ever done", and she loves the freedom and flexibility of running a business.

While she has experienced doubt from some customers when she turns up at their door - and has even once been mistaken for the receptionist - "once you start working and you show you're confident and you know what you're doing, they're okay".

She says the explosion of content online has "definitely helped" with broadening attitudes to women taking up DIY or a trade.

Anna Moynihan set up TaskHer, a platform connecting female tradies with customers who need jobs done, after feeling frustrated when tradesmen she had booked for renovation work would address her husband rather than her.

Five years ago she says she couldn't find any stock photographs of tradeswomen to use for marketing. Even the word "tradeswoman" would get autocorrected to "tradesman".

"It's those little things that, you know, ultimately you don't feel welcome into that environment.

"It's already hard enough to become a tradeswoman, a woman in an industry where you're massively under-represented."

Enquiries on the site have more than doubled so far this year compared to 2025, while the number of tradeswomen signing up has almost quadrupled, Anna says.

People might prefer a tradeswoman for a range of reasons - industry surveys suggest they may feel more at ease with a woman entering their home, external, feel a woman would be more respectful, or want to support women working in traditionally male roles.

Despite the buzz, women make up a tiny proportion of the UK's construction workforce - around 4%, according to the Federation of Master Builders.

But there are encouraging signs. One in 10 people who started a construction apprenticeship in 2024-25 was a woman, up from around one in 14 five years earlier.

DIY influencer Jasmine hopes women who see online content such as hers will be inspired to give a project a go, or consider entering a trade.

"The more women who are seen online doing these sorts of things, the more normal it becomes."

Anna agrees. "You can't be what you can't see, and anything that shows women and girls that they can do something is fantastic."

articles.title: One of the five men arrested near RAF Fairford called 999 himself
articles.text:
One of five men arrested near RAF Fairford in the early hours of Sunday morning had dialled 999 himself, the BBC understands.

The suspect called the police at 00:45 BST, almost an hour before a female farmer also dialled 999 after seeing men in balaclavas.

The five were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later terrorism offences after three vans were spotted, sparking a major security incident around the Gloucestershire base which the US military operates.

They were released on bail on Monday in what police described as an "investigative decision" "grounded in experience and strategy".

Police say a quantity of petrol but no explosive devices were found during searches of the vans.

Police were alerted to "three suspicious vehicles" in Whelford, a village which lies directly east of the base, by the farmer.

She told the BBC it was "pure luck" she had spotted them, having arrived home to find the road blocked and a "large group of hooded and masked men".

"I believe that my 999 call foiled whatever plans they had," she said.

A bomb disposal team arrived on scene shortly afterwards and a 400m (1,312ft) cordon was put in place.

But Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, told reporters on Tuesday that the police response that morning had been due to "a range of information".

Police cordons near the base are expected to be completely lifted on Wednesday, while residents from the 85 homes evacuated on Sunday have been allowed to return to their properties.

The five men are all UK nationals aged between 23 and 25. Four of them live in Westminster and one in Camden, and searches of their homes are now complete.

Taylor previously said their bail was "subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others" as they remained under investigation.

"The safety of the public is at the forefront of our investigative decision-making, and this was certainly the case yesterday," he said on Tuesday.

"I understand why this development was surprising to some, but I would like to reiterate that this is an investigative decision and one which is grounded in experience and strategy."

The RAF base has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force for decades.

In recent months, US bombers have taken off from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.

US President Donald Trump on Tuesday told journalists he was "disappointed" the five men had been released on bail.

articles.title: How did the RAF Fairford incident go from 'suspected bomb plot' to police bail?
articles.text:
On Sunday morning, the world was watching as drama unfolded in the village of Whelford.

Before sunrise, residents were called from their beds and told to evacuate as a huge police operation unfolded in the village, which is next door to RAF Fairford, a base used by the US Air Force.

One villager managed to take a picture of five men sitting on the ground, stripped to the waist, handcuffed and under armed guard.

They were arrested for offences under the Explosives Act. But now counter-terrorism detectives say no explosives were found in their three vans, only an "accelerant" - petrol.

What some newspapers called a "suspected bomb plot" ended in the suspects being bailed. So what was going on?

The US President Donald Trump asserted that the men had been trying to do "big damage" to the base. "We had them under view for a long time, and we got them," he declared.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said: "What could have happened in the UK over the weekend is a very serious situation. It's one that clearly involved the hands of a foreign actor."

But in a veiled criticism of that, the head Counter Terrorism Policing in the UK Laurence Taylor said that the worry that a lot of people had been experiencing had been "heightened by the international commentary".

He also defended his detectives' decision to give the suspects police bail with "very strict conditions". This had been criticised by President Trump.

Taylor said it was an "investigative decision and one which is grounded in experience and strategy".

This suggests there were good tactical reasons for releasing the men on bail, perhaps to encourage their cooperation.

In truth, once it became clear that the military remote-controlled robots that were used found no explosives in the vans, only petrol, the investigation inevitably changed.

It left detectives with five men from London in their 20s in police custody who had simply been found parked up near the air base in the middle of the night in suspicious circumstances and with some petrol - but little other usable concrete evidence.

It might have been hard to persuade a senior officer or a magistrate to extend the suspects' detention without something more definite.

The men were being held under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act (PACE), not the Terrorism Act (TACT). This meant detectives had the option to use police bail with strict conditions, but could not hold the men for 14 days, which they could have done if TACT had been used.

For a while it was unclear whether the men were already being watched by undercover surveillance teams when they were spotted by villagers in the dead of night, or whether the villagers really were the first people to alert the police.

Taylor has now given some assistance on this, saying the response on Sunday morning was "due to a range of information that we received", suggesting the police had some other intelligence

Certainly security had been visibly stepped up at the base in the preceding days, so certainly there had been some intelligence about a possible attack. Elite firearms officers were very quick to respond to the villagers' 999 calls.

Both counter-terrorism and military sources have told me that this story is still quite near the beginning, raising the possibility that detectives are trying to identify some kind of "controlling hand" behind the presence of the suspects in Whelford with their petrol.

That leaves a number of options open:

The men could be entirely innocent and able to give a good explanation for being in Whelford on Sunday

They could have been paid or tricked into moving the vehicles and the petrol, but unaware of who they were working for

Or they could have been part of a plot which was interrupted before it reached a more dangerous phase

That is why the next bit of the counter-terrorism investigation is so vital.

By examining mobile phones and computers, tracking vehicles, searching addresses, and using the covert techniques of MI5, GCHQ and US intelligence, detectives are trying to build a clearer picture.

On that critical investigation rests the decision over whether to arrest anyone else, whether to charge the five men, and whether we ever find out the true story of the mysterious RAF Fairford plot.

articles.title: Household energy bills forecast to see biggest rise in four years
articles.text:
Household energy prices are set to soar in January, with a typical annual bill forecast to jump by £276, figures shared with the BBC reveal.

The 16% predicted increase would hit millions of households at the coldest time of year, and would mark the biggest rise in bills for four years.

The forecast from consultancy Cornwall Insight comes a day before prices go up under regulator Ofgem's October price cap and puts increased pressure on the government to support those who will struggle to pay.

Meanwhile, the boss of supplier EDF Simone Rossi has warned the UK is "walking into a second energy crisis" and called for an extension to the VAT cut on electricity which kicks in on Thursday.

About 20 million households in England, Scotland and Wales are on variable energy tariffs set by Ofgem's price cap, which puts a maximum price on each unit of gas and electricity.

Those homes will see a 4% increase in prices on Thursday, the equivalent of about £60 per year – or £5 per month – taking an annual bill to £1,723 for the typical household using both electricity and gas and paying by direct debit if this level was sustained for a year.

That rise would have been higher without the government's VAT cut, which knocks the equivalent of about £45 a year off a typical bill.

But forecasts show a far greater increase is possible for bills in January. Cornwall Insight said its latest forecast suggests the typical annual bill would rise to £1,999.

The forecast 16% rise will come at the worst time of year, according to Craig Lowrey, principal consultant at Cornwall Insight.

"These prices are going to hit households hard. January is already a difficult month for many, with cold weather and bank balances still recovering from Christmas," he said.

The predicted rise is the result of disruption of gas supplies owing to the conflict in the Middle East, and the resulting low gas storage levels in Europe. Rebuilding those stocks could mean high bills "well beyond the winter", the forecaster said.

Cornwall Insight has a strong track record on forecasts and is widely respected across the industry and politics. Similar forecasts have been made by energy suppliers.

This remains only a prediction at this stage. Ofgem will not announce the actual January price change until late November.

While an easing of tensions in the Middle East could lessen the pain for billpayers, the price setting period for the January cap is already halfway through.

With little sign of a truce or lower international energy costs, a big increase in prices for those not on a fixed tariff looks highly likely. Lowrey said a January rise was "all but certain".

That will be tough for people like Aaron Richards from Maidenhead.

"I try to eat less takeaways, work more overtime, and try to budget a bit better, but at the same time, we shouldn't have to," he said.

Aaron drives a diesel car, and so is paying record high prices to travel to and from work.

"I just feel like everything's going up. How far is it going to go? Someone's got to step in," he said.

"I know people who can't afford to heat their house and they're struggling at the moment. Housing and eating are two of life's essentials that everyone should have. It shouldn't be a challenge to have any of those things."

Among others calling for government help for struggling billpayers is Simone Rossi, chief executive of supplier EDF Energy.

Speaking exclusively to the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast, Mr Rossi said: "We are actually walking into a second significant energy crisis after the one we experienced just four years ago."

He said that the government should extend the cut in VAT on electricity bills from 5% to 0% beyond April, when it is due to expire.

He also urged ministers to give the go-ahead to the new Jackdaw gas field off the coast of Aberdeen, and the Rosebank oil field off Shetland.

The government has consistently said that it will consider ways to offer breathing space to billpayers on the cost of living.

Additional reporting by Oliver Smith and Paul Seddon. Graphics by Miguel Roca-Terry.

articles.title: Andy Burnham pledges pension triple lock changes to fund care reforms
articles.text:
Andy Burnham has set out his plan to transform Britain, including by ending the existing state pension triple lock from 2030 to help fund a new national care service.

In his first Labour Party conference speech as prime minister, Burnham also said he wants to pave the way for greater public control over housing, water and energy services, and potentially reform the UK's electoral system.

After days of questions over how to fund his social care reforms in England, Burnham pointed to changing the triple lock to generate "significant savings".

His plans would see the state pension increase every year at least by inflation or 2.5% - but remove the automatic annual link with average earnings.

In front of a packed hall and watched on by family and friends, Burnham spoke for more than an hour - at times pausing and appearing to hold back tears as he referred to his father, Roy, who died earlier this month.

Arriving on stage to the sound of "All Together Now" by Liverpool band The Farm, Burnham made the song title a theme of his speech.

He said he wanted to "draw a line on a decade of division" and to "stop doomscrolling on posts running Britain down".

Burnham also told conference that he wants to "put the country on a new path" and recalled his family's "working-class aspiration" and how the government wanted to "unlock" this for others.

There was an expectation that Burnham's time in Liverpool for his party's conference would see him flesh out his vision for the future of the country.

In the conference hall, he offered more details albeit with some of the proposals relating to the content of the Labour manifesto at the next general election rather than delivering immediate action.

Burnham's plan to offer free at the point of use social care in England is among those being developed so it can be put before voters in 2029. He said it would be "fully funded and not through borrowing".

Explaining his long-held ambition to make changes, he raised his family's experiences - including how his grandmother Kitty's engagement ring was "ripped from her finger and stolen in a care home".

He argued a national care service was a "landmark" policy that would be "as significant as the creation of the NHS itself and utterly essential to securing its future".

Before turning to the pension triple lock changes, Burnham accepted he may "pay a political price" by trying to make the reforms but argued "someone has to go through the pain barrier and rip the plaster off".

The triple lock was introduced in 2010 by the coalition government and designed to ensure the value of the state pension was not overtaken by the increase in the cost of living or the incomes of working people.

It means the state pension rates rise every April by either inflation, earnings growth or 2.5% - whichever is the highest.

Burnham said this will stay in place until 2030, at which point he would like to "adjust it".

He said: "The state pension will continue to rise every year at least by prices or 2.5%. And it will hold its value relative to earnings over time so that pensioners will always share in the rising prosperity of the nation.

"But this change will generate significant savings which we will use to build up our national care service.

"Some may not realise it but older people with nothing more than the state pension, or only a little more, can find themselves paying care charges today from that small income. Under my plan, this will no longer happen."

Officials have suggested the change could save £15bn a year by 2040.

Jonathan Cribb, deputy director at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said savings "are likely to be relatively small in the first few years, but rise substantially over time".

He also said "we should not expect this reform to save enough that it could fund universal social care in the next parliament".

Sharon Graham, general secretary of the Unite union, told the BBC she believed the government should have "pulled another lever", such as a wealth tax, rather than making changes to the triple lock.

The political backlash was immediate.

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said "more tax rises are inevitable" under Labour's plan, while Reform UK's Nigel Farage accused the PM of "launching an offensive against our elderly".

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said families "cannot wait until after another election and it can't be funded from the pockets of our poorest pensioners".

Elsewhere in his speech, Burnham said he wanted to repeal "Margaret Thatcher's ideological ban on public ownership of water companies".

The PM said legislation will be put before Parliament, adding the changes will "start a 10-year journey to a very different water system", which includes new powers for mayors to hold "companies to account".

Burnham said it will be made easier for councils to acquire private rented homes in poor condition if landlords refuse to take action after being issued warnings.

He said the government will change the law "if necessary".

Burnham also told delegates that "Brexit has done more harm than good" before he indicated he wanted to explore closer UK-EU ties.

Ahead of talks expected later this year with EU chiefs, Burnham said he would set out the "different options" for Britain's "long-term relationship" with the bloc.

He said: "I will see if we can find consensus around one, which will give us clarity about our position and the future of the continent that we live in."

To cheers in the hall, Burnham announced a national commission on electoral reform, which could result in changes to the current voting system for UK parliamentary elections.

He asked all political parties to contribute to the work of the commission, adding: "We will contest the next election with a manifesto commitment to change the electoral system so that everyone's vote counts and everyone's voice is heard."

In response, Skills Minister Baroness Smith of Malvern told the PA news agency: "Electoral reform isn't top of my list of priorities. Good luck to the commission. I shall be interested in what it comes out with."

Burnham also said he wants to "invest" in young people and change the education system and welfare system.

He said: "We will rebuild a system of comprehensive education in this country, with parity between academic and technical."

Burnham added there needs to be a "fundamental rethink" of the welfare system to fund new opportunities for young people.

Green Party leader Zack Polanski said the PM's conference speech contained little more than "half measures, reannouncements and tinkering".

articles.title: Chris Mason: Andy Burnham delivers deeply political speech with a personal core
articles.text:
The key thing to understand about Andy Burnham's speech is these were the words and the delivery of both a new prime minister and a grieving son.

Burnham is living through two life-shaping, even life-defining moments right now – becoming and adjusting to being prime minister during the final weeks of his dad Roy's life, and preparing his speech while dealing with the grief of his loss.

The funeral will take place in a few days' time.

Reflections on his dad's life and influence formed the personal spine to this deeply political speech, which ranged far and wide.

Labour figures are enthused that they now have a leader with what they see as a clear sense of purpose that can be easily articulated.

The tacit, unflattering comparison with former PM Sir Keir Starmer is obvious.

What stood out in this speech was its breadth. His pitch could, very broadly, be divided into the short term - what he hopes to achieve before a general election; and the long term - the prospectus he is beginning to assemble to put to the country when polling day comes around inside the next three years.

The biggest ideas have the longest timeframe and, perhaps, the greatest need for a lengthy debate in their gestation.

Take the headline grabber: revamping social care in England. Previous attempts to do so, by both Labour and the Conservatives, haven't survived the intensity of a general election campaign, having been announced close to an election.

The aim of Burnham's plan is to seed a conversation now about what a new system might look like – the idea being that the argument is won in advance.

Let's see. The debate is only just beginning.

The plan to fund this by making increases in the state pension from 2030 less generous than they are now was more detailed than some expected at this stage.

The triple lock means the state pension currently increases annually in line with inflation, average wage growth or 2.5%, whichever is highest.

But from April 2030, if Labour win the next election, the annual earnings link will be dropped. It would, Labour figures say, be increased further if needed, to ensure that it stays above 30% of the full time average wage.

Knowing they would face blunt criticism about binning the existing triple lock – note the reaction of the Unite union and Labour's political rivals – it would appear the prime minister was keen to offer as much of what he hopes will be reassuring detail to many.

Also going into the next Labour manifesto, he said, a change in the Westminster voting system and – after a review to come – the idea of a closer relationship with the European Union.

How much closer, with what trade offs and prompting what reaction, we don't yet know.

And from the longer term stuff to the here and now – including housing reform in England, more public control of the water industry and the electricity grid.

There was an energy and sense of urgency to Burnham's pitch and without question he has created a battalion of dividing lines with Labour's political opponents which are likely to dominate the debate ahead.

His cabinet and many in his party are relishing the battle of ideas the prime minister has set up and is enthusiastically leaning into.

It was noteworthy that beyond a broad reference to Labour's opponents on the Right, the party's rivals didn't get a mention in a speech lasting more than an hour.

The question is: does he and his government have the capacity to deliver?

And do they have the capacity to convince you, the voter, they have a vision you regard as coherent, appealing and affordable?

You hardly need reminding of the backdrop that contributed to thwarting many of his recent, many predecessors: a persistently sclerotic economy and a persistently turbulent international picture, for starters.

Neither will make turning all of this into a reality straightforward.
