articles.title: OpenAI unveils AI assistant 'dots' while safety worries delay new model
articles.text:
OpenAI on Tuesday unveiled "dots," a new artificial intelligence (AI) assistant they say can proactively carry out tasks on a user's behalf.

At its annual developer day in San Francisco, chief executive Sam Altman referred to "dots" as "remarkably capable, always-on agents that can handle really anything you can think of."

At the same time, OpenAI president Greg Brockman and other tech leaders held a meeting with President Donald Trump as the firm faces intense scrutiny after internal tests of its AI agents revealed unexpected and occasionally harmful actions.

Dots, however, were pitched as brightly coloured cute cartoons meant to function as digital assistants for people with busy lives.

The dots, Altman said, "can handle really anything you can think of."

A glossy video was shown during the event, with people speaking to and naming animated versions of their "dots," then giving them various tasks, like building a website and booking afterschool activities for their children.

Speaking about "my dot," Altman almost entirely eschewed referring to the tool as an agent, which has been in common use for years. AI agents are essentially AI chatbots that are programmed to operate somewhat autonomously.

"You just give your dot a responsibility... and your dots will just get to work and keep working," Altman added.

OpenAI's event on Tuesday took place as President Donald Trump held a White House lunch with tech leaders and House Speaker Mike Johnson.

Trump repeated his belief that AI companies should regulate themselves.

He also said they had discussed creating a ten person committee to oversee the sector, adding there would be "tremendous self-policing"

Some researchers and company heads have called for a slowdown in AI development as more instances of breaches by AI firms' models become public.

"We need to navigate the centrist path," Altman told the BBC during a question and answer session with reporters on Tuesday.

"I am hopeful that the industry will figure out a more sensible, more pragmatic stance than has been exhibited by some of the members of our industry," he added, declining to specify particular company names or leaders.

The day prior to OpenAI's event, the company said it was delaying the launch of its latest model due to certain safety issues that showed up during internal testing.

Since July, the company has been dealing with a series of issues with its AI agents acting improperly. It has faced unprompted hacking into the AI platform Hugging Face, posting to third-party websites images that AI agents took from ChatGPT user chats, and accessing non-public information maintained by the Australian government.

OpenAI, as well as rival AI firm Anthropic, previously delayed public release of certain AI models due to potential risks, mostly pertaining to cybersecurity or hacking concerns.

On Tuesday, Altman raised the possibility of "a legitimate loss of control" to an AI system, adding "and you can imagine where we have too much concentration of power in a small number of companies or one company or person or country or whatever".

Both OpenAI and Anthropic are expect to be listed on the public stock market in the coming months. Anthropic likely will do so this year, while OpenAI is poised for 2027.

Altman said he was eager for his company to sell shares in public markets.

"I think it's bad for the world if OpenAI waits too long to go public," Altman told reporters. "I want people to be able to part in the upside of AI."

Both companies have lately been clear that they believe AI poses a genuine risk on a large scale, be it to public infrastructure or public safety.

Speaking last week to the UN, Altman pleaded for "national and international" AI standards on measuring the capabilities of an AI tool, assessing related risks, AI safeguards, and the degree to which human oversight over such tools is maintained.

Dario Amodei, the head of Anthropic, told the UN that if the speeding development of AI was not properly managed and overseen, future versions of the technology "could be a risk to humanity as a whole."

articles.title: OpenAI scraps rollout of new AI model over safety concerns
articles.text:
OpenAI has announced it will not release its latest AI model due to safety concerns.

Its GPT-6.1 Astra system, which performs tasks like browsing the web and using apps by itself, "didn't quite meet the bar" of the company's standards, according to Saachi Jain, head of safety systems at OpenAI.

The ChatGPT-maker also issued an update on incidents that occurred in June but were not made public until last week, where its models accessed Australian government websites and systems without authorisation.

It comes as breaches by major AI firms' models intensify the debate about risks posed by the tech - with Anthropic underlining its concerns AI might threaten humanity as it prepares to go public.

Reuters reported on Tuesday that the AI developer - which makes ChatGPT-rival Claude - plans to warn potential investors in its Initial Public Offering (IPO) that the tech may pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity", according to a prospectus it has seen, external.

Despite the stark warnings, the company is expected to become one of the most valuable in the world when it goes public.

"I think it's kind of crazy that companies are continuing to push forward with developing these capabilities when we've already seen over the last couple of months of incidents that they're nowhere near safe and controlled enough", said Jess Whittlestone, a senior advisor on AI policy for the Centre for Long-Term Resilience think tank.

Top AI leaders including Anthropic boss Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman have urged the industry to slow the pace of development.

OpenAI's decision, first reported by the Wall Street Journal, is a rare instance of a major AI developer pulling a new release over safety concerns.

The model fell short in terms of "staying within scope and authorisation and how it communicates back to the user about the type of work it's done," Jain said.

"We want to make sure our model development is safe no matter whether that's in the company, or when we ship it to users. But when we ship it to users, we have an extremely high bar in terms of safety and alignment," she added.

The flagship GPT-6 Astra agentic model was released in September and specialises in complex reasoning and executing tasks autonomously. OpenAI said it was the result of "years of research and big bets".

OpenAI is set to hold its annual DevDay developer conference in San Francisco on Tuesday, where it is expected to make several announcements. It is unclear if a new version of Astra will be among them.

The company's security controls have come under intense scrutiny after several high-profile incidents involving its technology.

It is not the first time a large AI developer has pulled or held back a new model.

Earlier this year, Anthropic said it would not publicly release a powerful Claude model, Mythos, because it was too good at finding dormant software bugs.

The company released a version of that model to the public several months later.

OpenAI meanwhile said in 2019 it would not be "too dangerous" to release one of its GPT models, now used to power its tools like ChatGPT.

The firm's decision to not publicly release the latest version of Astra was "a welcome sign that they are taking safety concerns seriously," said Prof Tony Cohn, foundational models theme lead at the Alan Turing Institute.

But he added that "safety should not be left purely in the hands of the developers: it should also be monitored and verified through independent government-approved regulators".

Prof Gina Neff, of the Minderoo Centre for Technology and Democracy at the University of Cambridge, said OpenAI's announcement showed "how much more the company needs to do to make their AI products safe".

She told the BBC it was "critical" to have independent tests of AI models by labs like the UK's AI Security Institute - which evaluates frontier systems on a voluntary basis - because "these companies have proven that we can't rely solely on them for our safety".

Last week, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced that a rogue OpenAI agent had hacked into government websites and systems in June in what experts said was the first known case of its kind in the world.

Albanese criticised OpenAI for notifying the Australian government through a generic email address rather than making direct contact with officials.

OpenAI said in a statement on Tuesday that it was sorry for the incident and that it "should have handled our response better".

Services Australia, the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, the Victorian Department of Health and the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare were all affected, OpenAI clarified.

The firm said it launched investigations as soon as it became aware of issues in mid-August and notified the affected organisations between 10 and 24 September.

"Our aim was to give affected agencies a detailed account once our investigation was complete," OpenAI said, adding that it should have shared early findings more promptly and kept Australian authorities updated.

The pontiff, who said on Monday during a visit to France that AI "should be taken seriously", added he had read that Huang had suggested there could be a way to insert guardrails ‌into certain AI models.

"He's the same one, however, ⁠that says there should ⁠be no limits placed and no government regulation," said the Pope.

Nvidia declined to comment on the record.

US President Donald Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson are set to host tech executives at the White House later on Tuesday to discuss regulations around AI.

Trump has downplayed concerns about AI's risks as a "hoax", arguing that the US has sufficient laws in place and that the only "guardrails" the technology needs is a "strong and smart" president.

articles.title: Apple ordered to pay $5.7bn in haptic tech patent case
articles.text:
Apple has been ordered to pay $5.7bn (£4.3bn) in damages after a US jury found it had used another firm's tech without permission.

Audio firm Taction Technology claimed in 2021 that Apple had infringed two of its patents for haptics systems, which enable vibrations for actions such as receiving a message or pressing a button.

This tech is built into devices like the iPhone and Apple Watch.

Apple said it had not used Taction's vibration tech and would appeal the verdict.

"While we thank the jury for their consideration, we strongly disagree with today's verdict and the damages awarded, which are entirely unsupported by the facts," it said.

"Apple's Taptic Engine is fundamentally different from Taction's technology, which Taction's own testing of Apple's products confirmed during trial."

Haptics allow people to interact with devices by simulating the sense of touch or feel through vibrations.

They have become a hallmark of modern devices, with smartphones, watches and video game controllers among those containing small motors that move in response to specific electronic signals.

articles.title: OpenAI bots meddled with US government agencies, including SEC and Census
articles.text:
OpenAI has acknowledged that it alerted "dozens" of global institutions that their websites may have been meddled with by its AI bots acting improperly.

AI agents attempted to get information from "governments, universities, public agencies, and other institutions", including the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Census Bureau and Education Department, the company said.

The disclosures come days after Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced that OpenAI agents had breached non-public files on the website of its government-run health care scheme.

Since August, public fears have grown over the potentially serious, even life-threatening, impacts of AI tools falling outside of human control.

OpenAI said that some of the data was accessed by AI agents, essentially bots that are designed and trained to operate somewhat autonomously, which were working to find "authoritative sources of public information".

But the company noted that some of the bots went beyond that and worked to bypass security measures on websites.

When attempting to get information from the Census Bureau, for instance, AI agents used tools reserved for software developers to access it, the company said.

OpenAI said all of the government data accessed by bots was public.

However, it noted that information that its bots accessed from the SEC, which regulates the US stock market and protects investors, was later published by AI agents on another website. OpenAI says this action was not intended.

In other instances that OpenAI disclosed on Friday, its AI agents transferred data when it should not have.

Such activity resulted in at least 53 incidents where an OpenAI agent took an image from ChatGPT user activity and transferred it elsewhere.

The company said that in each instance of a user image being used and transferred by an AI agent, the user had opted in to allow OpenAI to train models using their data.

Nevertheless, OpenAI admitted: "This is not an appropriate use of this data."

It added that the leak of user images occurred before it had put in place new safeguards on AI training, and it was working to get all the user images transferred to any third-party removed.

Reuters first reported the expanded investigations. OpenAI also published details to its public blog.

In certain instances of the agent activity, OpenAI said the tools "bypassed" security controls of some websites.

In other instances, the AI agents showed "misalignment" in attempts to get at information from websites. Misalignment is a term used by AI companies and researchers to describe instances where an AI tool did something that it was not trained to do or was otherwise unintended.

OpenAI said that it was limiting identifying what entities were impacted because many had asked the company to not disclose details.

"Our goal is to give each organization the facts and defer to them on if and when to make the incident public," it said.

Not all of the instances involved in this incident were being considered a significant security breach, the company noted.

"Some organizations may review what we share and conclude that the information was intentionally public or that the model's interaction was not concerning," it explained. "Others may identify a design issue or security weakness they want to address."

While OpenAI and Anthropic have both said in recent weeks that they will bring third-party evaluators inside their companies to do real-time safety evaluations of AI tools and models, such evaluators have not yet arrived, as the BBC has reported.

OpenAI said on Friday that it is currently reviewing training activity by its AI agents and going back on a "month by month" basis from when the Hugging Face hack occurred.

"Most cases identified so far have been low severity, with limited or no evidence of meaningful impact," the company said. "Given the scale of the review required, and the need to verify each case, this work will take months to complete."

David Krueger, a professor of machine learning at University of Montreal and the founder of AI safety group Evitable, said on Friday that he was "deeply troubled" by the increasing number of AI-related safety incidents.

He called for "an immediate, indefinite, international moratorium" on AI development.

"We have yet to understand the extent of existing incidents, and future rogue AI scenarios could be catastrophic," Krueger said.

articles.title: Silent Hill Townfall: Iconic horror game gets a clever Scottish makeover
articles.text:
As I creep through the heavy fog of Silent Hill: Townfall, I'm met by an oddly familiar sight amid the terror - a sign for a Sunday roast.

For the first time, one of gaming's biggest horror franchises - created in Japan but traditionally set in the US - has come to the UK, set on a fictional Scottish island.

Jon McKellan, director at Glaswegian developers Screen Burn, told me taking on the mega brand was an "absolutely terrifying" prospect for the relatively small team.

As a fan of the games, I was keen to find out what one of the most iconic survival horror series looks like in Scotland - and whether it can live up to its legacy.

I played Silent Hill: Townfall, which was released on Thursday, on my PlayStation 5, and it ran well, though there have been some reports, external from others of performance issues.

Set in 1996, the game follows the plight of an American man called Simon Ordell, who washes up on St Amelia with a red hospital ID band around his wrist and an IV drip in his arm.

As is to be expected from the Silent Hill games, the real reasons why you're there and what's going on are teased as you progress through the story in a typically vague fashion.

In Townfall I walked past film-quality models of red pillar boxes, 20 mph speed limit signs and charity collection boxes shaped like guide dogs.

Not since 2006, when I had to storm Manchester Cathedral in Resistance: Fall of Man, have I felt an oddly patriotic attachment to game areas or objects.

To save the game, I had to use a phone, which often meant stepping inside a "coins and card" telephone box - a sight instantly familiar to anyone old enough to remember them on British streets.

Meanwhile, a level set in a council estate leans into the concrete starkness of the area's looming grey buildings.

While some may question why the main character is American rather than Scottish given the setting, there are narrative reasons why Simon is more of an outsider to this community, which are slowly drip-fed into cutscenes and in-game documents.

For the most part I was intrigued by the story, which, like many of the previous games, explores themes of trauma and guilt sensitively. This edition also touches on ideas around the impact of big corporations on small communities, which brought added relevance to the setting of an isolated seaside town.

I soon had to face the island's monsters - gnarled, fleshy beings with axe-like heads or mangled faces.

While St Amelia's inhabitants might not quite live up to the heights of Silent Hill 2's mannequins for sudden frights, their speed and general nastiness were still enough to make me want to run away as fast as possible.

Even when I picked up weapons such as a plank of wood or a steel pipe, a series staple, there was never much sense that I had the upper hand.

These all degrade over time, and though I did eventually get a gun, bullets are scarce, meaning I still had to sneak around rather than face threats head-on.

"We don't do jump scares, really," said McKellan - although I can think of a few alarming times playing the game I vehemently disagreed with that statement.

The fear is dialled up an extra notch by Byron Bullock's rich sound design, with the music swelling almost unbearably intensely when spluttering nasties stumbled closer.

Composer Pilotpriest, also known as Anthony Scott Burns, deserves recognition too for his hauntingly bleak soundtrack.

I think it says a lot that I closed every door I opened behind me in the game, in the naive hope it might stop monsters following - even at moments when there were none around.

Simon soon picks up a handheld CRT device to help with sneaking - a clever updated version of another staple of the Silent Hill series: the crackling radio.

This piece of retro tech - basically a small portable TV - gives you a fuzzy image of nearby monsters on its screen, so you have some idea of where they are in order to avoid them, though it can get a little fiddly if there are several nearby.

"I think it lends itself well to horror when the technology is a bit frail, a bit outdated," said McKellan.

"You don't feel safe when those kinds of things are fragile."

Later sections where you rely on even cruder tech to spot enemies ratchet up the tension further, at the expense of making the gameplay much slower.

Thankfully, there are often other cues as to the whereabouts of your fleshy foes, such as flickering lights and their awful, gurgling cries.

Townfall is not the first time the series has strayed away from the original game's location in America, 2025's Silent Hill f was set in 1960s rural Japan.

This sparked a conversation about whether a game can be part of the series yet not be set in or around the fictional eponymous town.

The series' lead producer at Konami Motoi Okamoto told me the team were looking at various areas to potentially set the next games, from "other parts of Europe" to "Latin America".

Games journalist and self-proclaimed "Silent Hillian" Vikki Blake told me the latest game exceeded her expectations, though she's still not convinced these newer games truly fit under the Silent Hill name.

After my playthrough, I can see why Konami are pushing ahead with the idea to let other studios breathe new life into the franchise and take it to different destinations.

Townfall is a brutal, grim journey - uneven in parts, but clever - and full of immense tension and inventive game design, the kind that is needed to push a nearly 30-year-old franchise forward.

Okamoto has also expressed his desire, external to release a Silent Hill game every year - whether that be a remaster, remake, or entirely new material.

If more new studios can keep the games feeling as fresh as this, we may eventually become like one of the series' many troubled protagonists – forgetting why we ever needed the titular town at all.

articles.title: Agents fearful and angry after 'dangerous' FBI data breach
articles.text:
Current and former FBI agents have spoken to BBC News of their shock, fear and anger following a hack that appears to have exposed the private and personal information of the agency's entire workforce.

"This is really bad for our undercover agents," says one former FBI agent, who fears for the safety of his colleagues.

The former cyber investigator is in a group chat with current agents who are worried their personal information could soon be freely available online to criminals and hostile nation-state hackers.

He says staff fear they could be targeted, or that criminals could use the data to create highly convincing phishing attempts, scams or demands for bribes.

The hacking group ShinyHunters is threatening to publish the stolen databases and documents within four days unless its demands are met.

Some agents are also concerned about the risk of physical attacks from cyber criminals they have investigated.

"One of the things we are discussing in the group chat is 'violence-as-a-service' attacks from young online gangs," says the former worker.

"They could use this information to harass an FBI agent who has worked on their cases."

Groups similar to ShinyHunters - believed to be an English-speaking gang - have in the past been linked to swatting incidents, and even petrol bomb attacks against law enforcement officers and rivals.

Swatting is a phenomenon so-called because perpetrators make calls that prompt armed police units - called Swat teams in the US - to swoop in on victims.

The group claims it breached FBI systems on Monday and later posted details of the attack on its darknet site.

The FBI has not responded to requests for comment.

However, on Wednesday the agency acknowledged the breach - saying it was "aggressively investigating" how it occurred.

For Michael McPherson, a former FBI agent who is now senior vice president of security operations at cyber firm ReliaQuest, the hack presents "a security threat which cuts to the core of agent safety, particularly their families".

He says agents understand the "inherent risks" that come with the job.

"But this incident reportedly includes personal data such as home addresses and contact information, which could expose family members who are normally insulated from the threats associated with such a career," McPherson says.

ShinyHunters shared samples of the alleged stolen data with reporters, along with an extortion demand.

The samples appear genuine and include names, addresses, phone numbers, badge numbers, job titles and information about spouses.

The records appear to relate to thousands of agents, including senior officials such as deputy directors.

The criminals also appear to possess highly sensitive medical information relating to thousands of special agents.

BBC News has seen samples of stolen "fitness-for-work" medical examinations containing information such as blood and urine test results, along with doctors' notes mentioning conditions including a "shellfish and banana allergy".

Agents' full names and addresses, as well as references to medical issues including "blood in the urine" and "high cholesterol" are now in the criminals' hands.

Cynthia Kaiser, who was the Deputy Director of Cyber at the FBI and now leads the Research Centre at Halcyon says ShinyHunters appear to already have lost control of some of the data which is circulating in various online groups of cyber researchers and could lead to harm even before the main tranche is published.

"A lot of the damage may already be done, and as we have seen in past FBI data breaches, that information continues to circulate the dark web years later," she said.

There are also concerns about the breach's national security implications, such as staff becoming targets for recruitment efforts by hostile foreign intelligence services.

Alongside fear, many of those who spoke to the BBC expressed anger at the FBI for allowing the data to be stolen.

The hack is particularly embarrassing from a technical perspective because ShinyHunters is not generally regarded as a highly sophisticated hacking group.

One former cyber agent said FBI staff were furious about the "sloppy and lazy security failures" that allegedly enabled the breach.

There is also confusion about how to handle any fallout if data is published next week, as threatened.

The FBI appears unlikely to comply with the extortion demands, and the hackers have indicated they intend to post the information on their darknet site.

Unusually, the group is not demanding money. Instead, it wants the FBI to retract an advisory published in May, which it claims "offended" them.

"The agency leadership is lost," the former cyber investigator tells me.

He says staff have been advised to sign up to a service called DeleteMe, which helps remove personal information from data broker websites - a response he feels is inadequate.

There is also embarrassment that a prolific group of young cyber criminals has repeatedly managed to evade law enforcement while carrying out a string of high-profile hacks.

ShinyHunters has been linked to numerous extortion attacks, including on Rockstar Games and the education platform Canvas.

The group regularly communicates with reporters via Telegram, where members often boast about their activities.

"The bureau doesn't know what to do with teenage cyber criminals," one former agent says.

McPherson says there is no doubt the FBI is taking the incident extremely seriously.

He expects the agency to draw on its extensive network of partners and resources "to make this group suffer the consequences for this brazen and taunting attack".

Kaiser added that the hackers have been "reckless and foolish" and warned them to expect "a significant effort by the FBI to quickly bring them to justice."

articles.title: Special agents' blood and urine test results stolen in FBI hack
articles.text:
Cyber-criminals who hacked the FBI say they have extremely sensitive medical data for thousands of its special agents.

BBC News has seen samples of the stolen "fitness-for-work" medical examinations, which contain information such as blood and urine test results, and doctors' notes mentioning conditions such as a "shellfish and banana allergy".

The records include agents' full names and addresses, as well as references to medical concerns including 'blood in the urine' and 'high cholesterol'.

Experts say the hack - which the FBI is investigating - could leave agents vulnerable to scams, blackmail and targeted attacks, as well as help criminals impersonate law enforcement officers.

"The list maps thousands of agents against their medical and fitness records," said Etay Maor, vice-president of threat intelligence at Cato Networks.

"Passwords can be reset if stolen, but medical records cannot, so once this data is out, it stays compromised for good. That permanence, applied across an entire workforce, is what makes this leak so serious."

The FBI has not responded to requests for comment. However, on Wednesday it acknowledged the breach and said it was "aggressively investigating" how it happened.

The cyber-criminal group ShinyHunters claims it breached FBI systems on Monday, and later posted details of the attack on its darknet site.

The group also shared samples of the alleged stolen data with reporters, along with an extortion demand.

Unusually, the hackers are not demanding money. Instead, they are seeking a retraction of an FBI advisory published in May, which they claim "offended" them.

The samples shared with journalists appear genuine and include names, addresses, phone numbers, badge numbers, job titles and information about spouses.

The records appear to relate to thousands of agents, including senior officials such as deputy directors.

Professor Ciaran Martin, the former head of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre, has described the hack - if confirmed - "as serious as it gets when it comes to data breaches."

The news agency Reuters reports that some of the data includes information on agents, external involved in investigations relating to Russia, China and drug cartels.

Reporting by 404 Media suggests details of a previously little-known FBI hacking unit may also have been exposed, external.

It was initially thought the breach affected the FBI's 38,000 current employees, but the hackers now claim the number could be far higher.

The group says it underestimated the scale of the data theft and now claims to hold sensitive information on around 60,000 current and former FBI staff.

Jamie Akhtar, chief executive and co-founder of CyberSmart, said the hackers' claims should be treated with caution but that the breach appeared to be extremely concerning.

"Such data could be used for highly convincing phishing, impersonation, identity fraud, blackmail or even operations targeting law-enforcement personnel, making the potential implications particularly serious," he said.

The hackers, who communicate with reporters in English via the messaging service, Telegram, say they will publish the full dataset in five days unless the FBI meets their demands.

ShinyHunters is an international hacking collective that has been active since 2019 and has been linked to a number of high-profile cyber-attacks, including incidents affecting Rockstar Games and the education platform Canvas.

The group claims it exploited a vulnerability in an Oracle cloud storage system used by the FBI, gaining access to multiple platforms including FBIJobs, FBI BEAST, which handles background checks on employees and applicants, FBI MedLink, which stores medical records, and FBI BICS, which contains investigative information.

In a statement posted on X, the FBI said it was still trying to determine whether the hackers had breached its systems directly or compromised a third-party provider.

"We are actively and aggressively investigating this matter and working closely with those third-party providers that support FBIJobs.gov to mitigate any and all risk," the statement said.

articles.title: US backs Elon Musk's bid to overturn €120m EU fine against X
articles.text:
The US government is seeking to join Elon Musk's legal challenge to overturn a €120m (£105m) EU fine against X over its blue tick badges.

In December 2025, the European Commission said the platform "deceives users" by allowing people to pay for a blue verified check mark, because it is not "meaningfully verifying" who is behind the account.

But US Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate said on Thursday that the commission had "inappropriately attempted" to expand its reach to American companies outside its control.

Musk, who spent millions helping elect Donald Trump and other Republicans, has previously claimed EU tech regulation "inhibits progress" for companies.

The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has filed an application, external with the EU's General Court in support of Musk's and X's attempts to dismiss ​the case.

It claims that under a section of law in the Statute of the Court of Justice of the EU, a state may intervene in disputes before the court if it "can establish an interest in the result of the case to the court".

The DOJ said the US "has a clear interest" in ensuring any decision by the commission was applied consistently with "how territorial jurisdiction is generally understood in international law".

It also wants to make sure it would not "otherwise prejudice" US-headquartered digital services that "contribute significantly" to its economy.

In a press briefing on Friday, external, European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said it was "ready to defend" its position in court.

He added that the commission had an "solid case" at its disposal, due to the alleged breach of its Digital Services Act.

In addition to its use of blue ticks, EU regulators had accused X of failing to provide transparency around its adverts and denying researchers access to public data.

Henna Virkkunen, the regulator's executive vice-president for tech sovereignty, said at the time of the fine's issue it was "holding X responsible for undermining users' rights and evading accountability".

"Deceiving users with blue checkmarks, obscuring information on ads and shutting out researchers have no place online in the EU," she said.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) had criticised the EU regulator, accusing it of attacking and censoring US firms.

"The European Commission's fine isn't just an attack on X, it's an attack on all American tech platforms and the American people by foreign governments," Rubio wrote in a post on X.

"The days of censoring Americans online are over."

His remarks were reposted by Musk, who added "absolutely".

The European Commission denied targeting any specific nationality, stating it is simply protecting its digital and democratic standards to maintain its role as a global benchmark.

The action marked the Commission's first official non-compliance decision under the Digital Services Act (DSA), one of two mandatory rulebooks governing online platforms in the EU.

articles.title: MTV VMAs: Taylor Swift dominates but do music videos matter?
articles.text:
We're far from the days of blockbuster music videos playing back-to-back on TV channels like MTV.

Catchy hooks and sleek dance routines now dominate social media feeds, each hoping to stop people in their tracks long enough for them to give a new song a chance.

The evolution of this landscape was cemented last year when MTV axed five music channels in the UK after almost 40 years of rolling footage.

But despite the broadcaster reacting to the changes in viewing habits, its Video Music Awards (VMAs) still appear to hold power over music A-listers.

Pop music heavyweights, including Taylor Swift, Madonna and Charli XCX, were among those who turned up on Sunday to accept prizes and deliver dramatic performances.

Cinematographer Melissa Cofie tells BBC Newsbeat that while these award shows "may seem very performative to others", they are "so important" to those in the music industry.

"The sleepless nights, the months, the weeks that it takes to put together a music video, it's almost as much work as you would put into a film itself," she says.

But do music videos still hold the same importance for fans as they once did?

Cofie, who has directed music videos, feels their purpose has evolved over the last couple of decades.

For her, they're more of a way to "connect with artists" and for them to express their vision, rather than a crucial part of their press run like they were in the 2000s.

Pop stars like Swift, Sabrina Carpenter and Olivia Rodrigo are among those who still lean on videos heavily to build out the visual world for each of their albums' eras.

Swift, who broke the record for most MTV VMA wins ever last weekend, is known for big budget productions which fans trawl through for Easter eggs - clues that could point to something else she has planned.

She also often enlists the help of her star-studded contact book, with her recent video for Opalite jam-packed with famous faces, including Graham Norton, Lewis Capaldi, Cillian Murphy, Domhnall Gleeson and Jodie Turner-Smith.

However, the music video was released exclusively on Spotify and Apple Music in February, and did not appear on YouTube until 48 hours later.

Industry analysts speculated at the time that the exclusivity period was due to a change in the US chart rules, where songs streamed on YouTube will no longer count towards the Top 100.

This change came into place in January, with YouTube saying it was ending its decade-long partnership with Billboard, external as it claimed the chart uses an "outdated formula that weights subscription-supported streams higher than ad-supported".

"This doesn't reflect how fans engage with music today and ignores the massive engagement from fans who don't have a subscription," it added.

And while most artists don't have Swift-level budgets to start with, this change may have further discouraged US artists' to throw a lot of money into creating elaborate music videos.

However, in international markets like the world of K-Pop, creating visually aesthetic music videos featuring polished choreography has become essential when promoting the act to a global audience.

The genre's superstars like BTS and Blackpink often also release dance practice videos and behind-the-scenes clips alongside traditional music videos.

These variations offer them more content to clip up for social media, and also helps drive up their streaming numbers and global chart positions.

Cofie feels the rise of platforms like TikTok, Instagram and YouTube has "100%" changed the way videos are consumed and therefore, how they are created.

But she doesn't see this as a "blow" to the industry and isn't "discouraged that things are changing so quickly".

"It kind of pushes us to think: 'Okay, how can each scene, each still be the one that captures people's attention?'," she says.

"We don't have five minutes anymore. We've actually got two minutes, sometimes less.

"I think it pushes us as creatives to think how can we get the point across quickly in the best way possible."

Gener8ion and Swedish rapper Yung Lean's cinematic music video for their collaboration track Storm is a testament to how a short mesmerising visual moment can make a song go viral online.

The scene from within the full video sees Lean, acting as a teenage bully, stand amongst a group of dancers who are also dressed in school uniforms as they perform hypnotic, synchronised choreography, external.

They recreated the routine at the VMAs, and while it lost out on the coveted video of the year award to Swift's The Fate of Ophelia, clips of the performance once again have flooded social media.

Cofie admits it has been "really tough" to come up with "new creative ideas" like this since short clips have boomed post-pandemic, but says she is continually inspired by new music videos.

And her advice to artists and crews who still want to create music videos?

"It's cliche, but just to continue being creative and just exploring every corner of your mind, any idea that you have, just do it," she says.

"Don't worry that it's already been done and it's not original because each and every person's interpretation or perspective is different."

articles.title: Blue Lights: The police drama hitting home in Northern Ireland
articles.text:
"Whether it's your friends or your family, everybody has their own relationships with, and viewpoints on, the police," says Dearbháile McKinney, star of BBC drama Blue Lights.

The Londonderry actress and her co-star Katherine Devlin, who also grew up in Northern Ireland, say relationships between police and communities there were at the forefront of their minds as they prepared for filming.

The Bafta-winning series follows police officers working at the fictional Blackthorn Station in Belfast.

But, for many watching, the drama feels all too real.

The difficulty police in Northern Ireland still face was thrown into focus this weekend by the long-running dispute over the controversial Garvaghy Road parade route when officers had to prevent a march by Protestant Orangemen through a largely Catholic area.

Many scenes in Blue Lights highlight the distrust of, and hostility towards, the police in some communities.

Warning: This article includes spoilers for the first three seasons of Blue Lights.

Devlin plays Annie Conlon, whose storyline deals with her having to move away from home as a result of death threats because she's from a Catholic family.

"We do have similarities - she comes from a Catholic background and so do I," Devlin tells BBC Newsbeat. "I know girls like Annie.

"But I've realised we're different in a lot of ways. Mainly, to be honest with you, I wouldn't go into the police."

Devlin says that forming Annie's character was about trying to understand why she decided to become an officer and "for that to be the crux of her story".

"I think a huge thing with this season is the idea of home and what home means to her," she says.

"Just battling that inner dialogue that she has with 'is it all worth it?'

"Especially her being a Catholic and the intricacies of that and the politics of that.

"It's heavy stuff and she has to really think about it."

The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) had its lowest number of Catholic applicants in more than a decade earlier this year, with some pointing to "fear and apprehension" in those communities putting them off joining the police.

One of the force's aims when it was founded in 2001 was to build broader community support and increase Catholic officers.

At the time, only 8% of the force was from that background. It's now at 32%.

In a statement sent to Newsbeat, Chief Constable Jon Boutcher said the PSNI was "totally committed to being more representative of the communities we serve".

"I am deeply concerned at persistent and often unjustified criticism and the outdated and unsupported views of dissident paramilitaries remaining as barriers to people seeing themselves having a career in the police," he said.

Boutcher said he "absolutely" accepted the PSNI needed to do more to diversify its recruitment but could only do so if "people in all communities in Northern Ireland see policing as a career for them".

He said the force planned to launch a new student officer recruitment campaign "in the coming weeks".

Blue Lights is filmed locally and on set in east Belfast you can spot the attention to detail, right down to the information leaflets at a police station reception area and case folders on officers' desks.

"It's really lovely just to see the amount of people who see themselves in the characters," Devlin says.

"And [mention] how complex the characters are. How real and human they are."

It's something McKinney considered in how she plays Aisling Byrne.

Aisling struggled with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) in the last series, something Dearbháile says she spoke to real-life officers about.

"They've had to witness some horrific things and been left with PTSD and trauma that they just have to learn to live with," she says.

"It's the reality here. It would be ignorant to not think about that."

Aisling's condition puts a strain on her relationship with Tommy Foster, played by Nathan Braniff, who is then faced with the decision whether to report her to their bosses so she can get help.

And while Braniff says Blue Lights often deals with heavy themes, he believes it does a good job at showing what Northern Ireland is really like.

"It shows that Northern Ireland's moving forward and changing all the time."

One thing that's changed for the fourth series is the public interest when the actors are filming scenes in Belfast city centre.

"After having lived here my whole life, it's funny walking down the streets of Belfast and bumping into people that I know wearing my full police costume," Braniff says.

"The support for the show here is unmatched."

Frank Blake, who plays Shane Bradley, is one of the few actors who isn't from Northern Ireland but he says he felt the same welcome, thanks mainly to a scene where his character opens up about his love of a certain Westlife song.

"We were shooting in town, and someone drove past blaring World of Our Own out of the speakers," he says.

"I've long been a Westlife fan and it was great craic. It's so funny seeing how it really took off."

Series four of Blue Lights starts at 21:00 BST on BBC One and is available to watch on iPlayer.

articles.title: Celebrity Traitors star Michael Sheen says being an actor will be a 'disadvantage'
articles.text:
Michael Sheen has said he thinks being an actor will be a disadvantage while he is on Celebrity Traitors.

The 57-year-old is among the stars who will go head to head in the second series of the BBC reality game spin-off.

A total of 21 presenters, comedians, actors and musicians will try their hand at being traitors and faithfuls in the show, which airs on 1 October.

The Hollywood actor from Port Talbot said he wanted to participate because he is a "big fan" of the show and wanted to be in the castle after previously filming in the area.

Speaking about how his public persona may affect how others perceive and treat him on the show, the actor said: "Well, I do think it's a disadvantage to be an actor because people immediately go, 'oh well, he pretends for a living'.

"I don't think that is the case, because the whole point of acting is that you have to trick yourself into believing that what you're doing is true. If you are consciously aware that you're pretending or you're saying things that aren't true, then it's bad acting. It's just bad.

"Just for me being an actor, I think that's a disadvantage because people are already suspicious of that.

"Beyond being an actor, just my persona, I don't really know what people think about me. So, I don't know if it'll help or not."

Sheen portrayed the disgraced Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor in the 2024 Prime Video series, A Very Royal Scandal.

It was based on the 2019 BBC Newsnight interview conducted by Emily Maitlis with Mountbatten-Windsor regarding his relationship with Jeffrey Epstein, and became a defining moment in modern royal and media history.

Sheen has also starred in films including Frost/Nixon, The Damned United and The Special Relationship.

Sheen said: "I knew the area a bit [where Traitors is filmed in Scotland], and it is stunningly beautiful. It's a lovely place to be and the game is just fascinating.

"I think for a show to be so popular and to grab the cultural imagination so much, it has to have the ability to go beyond what its genre is.

"It somehow speaks to something a bit deeper, maybe. People get so absorbed in it."

articles.title: Somerset Booker Prize nominee praises former school teachers
articles.text:
An author whose latest book has been nominated for the prestigious Booker Prize said childhood boredom inspired his creativity.

Luke Kennard, who grew up in Chard in Somerset, has been shortlisted for Black Bag, which is based on an experiment involving an actor sitting in a bin bag at the back of a lecture hall.

He said, as a child, he had "quite a lot of time to practice" his creative passions.

Kennard also praised his teachers at the town's Holyrood Academy and said: "It just can't be exaggerated how much difference a teacher can make when they find a kid who has a passion for their subjects."

Kennard said growing up in a quiet town had an impact on his "creative impulse".

"You stay in your room playing the clarinet or writing a poem - there's a certain virtue to being a little bit bored sometimes, and just having to amuse yourself."

Kennard attended Holyrood Academy from 1992 to 1999 and studied both GCSE and A-level English Literature.

He added: "It was the teachers that I had who really encouraged my writing- that's quite foundational."

Kennard said the former head of English, Paul Coffman, would read his short stories during break times, and leave him notes and suggestions.

"He was the first person who really got me to take my writing seriously."

articles.title: Gisele Pelicot rape case play to be staged in central London
articles.text:
A play telling the "harrowing" story of the Gisele Pelicot rape case will be performed in London at a one-off event at London County Hall, on the South Bank.

Ms Pelicot's ex-husband, Dominique Pelicot, was jailed for 20 years for drugging and raping her, as well as allowing other men to rape her while she was unconscious, in abuse that lasted nearly a decade.

The 73-year-old, who waived her right to anonymity as a survivor of sexual abuse, said shame should fall on her abusers, not her.

Thirty actors and public figures will take part in the "documentary theatre" style performance, created from documents from the trial and psychiatric reports of the 51 men who were prosecuted.

The Pelicot Rape Trial created by Swiss director and playwright Milo Rau started as a stand-alone piece as part of the Festival d'Avignon, an arts festival in the town where the crimes took place.

The performance then travelled across cities in Europe, with only one show per location.

Milo Rau said: "It's about disentangling the story from the couple Gisèle and Dominique Pelicot – turning it into a story that belongs to all of us and at the same time to none of us."

In London, the piece is being put on at London County Hall, by the Young Vic Theatre, on 30 November.

The theatre's website said the performance is a "profoundly affecting piece of documentary theatre, comprised of testimonies and written accounts from the trial, (which) pays tribute to the ordinary woman who opened the way to change".

It added: "The Pelicot trial is undoubtedly the most publicised, discussed, and symbolic of our time.

"As a sociological study it shows that in a typical Western European city – the small town of Mazan in the south of France – perfectly ordinary men from all social classes and age groups are capable of perhaps the most extreme crime: the repeated rape of an unconscious woman."

Fifty men were found guilty of rape or sexual offences after a three-and-a-half-month trial.

Young Vic Theatre's artistic director and chief executive, Nadia Fall said: "Milo Rau's extraordinary testimonial piece The Pelicot Trial breaks out beyond our theatre walls to County Hall; a piece of confronting event-theatre which bears witness to the harrowing story of Gisèle Pelicot."

articles.title: Slipknot reveal world tour with Marilyn Manson as support act
articles.text:
Heavy metal band Slipknot have announced a new world tour, with Marilyn Manson due to appear as a support act.

The eight-piece group, known for performing in masks, will be joined by the US rock musician during their shows at London's Wembley Stadium and multiple dates of the South American leg of the tour.

Some fans have reacted angrily to the news and said they will not attend the shows over past sexual abuse accusations against the 57-year-old.

Manson, real name Brian Warner, has always strongly denied any allegations against him.

Thousands of fans replied to an Instagram post featuring the line-up for the London gigs, which also includes metalcore band Hatebreed.

While some posts expressed excitement at the support acts, many were critical of Manson's presence on the bill, describing it as "disappointing".

Others, who described themselves as long-time Slipknot fans, said they would not buy tickets for the show in protest at his appearance.

One wrote: "Would've loved to see this but there's literally nothing you could do to get my cash in Manson's pockets."

Another added the announcement was "such a disappointment" and they would not be attending.

However, others disagreed, with one pointing out the two acts have a "huge fanbase overlap" and describing Manson as a "perfect support act".

articles.title: Sir Ranulph Fiennes' relatives tell BBC it's 'very painful' not being able to visit him
articles.text:
Relatives of the British explorer Sir Ranulph Fiennes have said it is "very painful" he appears to have been hidden away from them.

Speaking to BBC Newsnight, his sister-in-law told the BBC that she did not know where he was, and nobody had been able to see him.

It has been alleged that Sir Ranulph, 82, has been admitted to a number of care homes under assumed names, after a family rift involving his second wife, Louise Millington-Cotes.

Louise Millington-Cotes did not immediately respond to the allegations, or the BBC's request for comment.

Cheshire Police have said they are aware of the concerns regarding Sir Ranulph, and are satisfied he is living in an appropriate setting with suitable care.

They said there were "no immediate safeguarding concerns".

Sir Ranulph has not been seen in public for nearly two years, just months after opening up about a diagnosis of Parkinson's disease, a progressive disorder affecting the brain, nervous system, and muscle control.

He was the first person to visit both north and south poles by surface means in the early 1980s and has been described by Guinness World Records as "the world's greatest living explorer".

Spending his childhood between the UK and South Africa, he joined the British Army after leaving school, going on to serve in the SAS.

Sir Ranulph's stepson, Alex Millington-Cotes, told BBC Newsnight he wanted to see the power of attorney "removed from my own mother" and placed in the hands of people who "have fully his best interests in mind".

"He's not an isolated type of person, and so to see him isolated now is very painful," he said.

Last week, he launched a crowdfunding campaign for legal fees to "locate and safeguard" the explorer, and so far it has raised almost £26,000.

He wrote that the fundraiser had been created as "a result of our concern and desperation" after trying "multiple avenues" to locate his stepfather.

Questions about Sir Ranulph's whereabouts grew in prominence after a report in the Telegraph earlier this month, external in which "members of his inner circle" raised concerns about his whereabouts.

The paper also reported concerns about Sir Ranulph have been raised with the Office of the Public Guardian (OPG), the government agency which helps people to stay in control of decisions about their health and finances.

In a statement to the BBC, an OPG spokesperson said: "We have a strict duty of confidentiality to all individuals who have made a lasting power of attorney, and it would be deeply inappropriate to comment on a specific case.

"We take all safeguarding concerns seriously and investigate thoroughly where there is the evidence and legal basis to do so."

articles.title: MTV VMAs: Taylor Swift breaks record as Madonna also wins
articles.text:
Taylor Swift took home the video of the year award as she became the most successful artist in the history of the MTV Video Music Awards on Sunday.

The singer went into the night tied with Beyoncé on 30 wins, and went on to score the night's top award for the visuals for her track The Fate of Ophelia, taken from her 2025 album The Life of a Showgirl.

The original Queen of Pop, Madonna, won artist of the year, best dance and best collaboration alongside Sabrina Carpenter for their dancefloor-filler Bring Your Love, which was the lead single from Madonna's 2026 album Confessions II.

Swift also received the inaugural award for artist director, having written and directed the 1990s infomercial parody video for another song, Opalite.

She dedicated her new award to the "ultimate showgirl", saying: "I think we were all very lucky to share this planet with Dolly Parton for a time".

The 36-year-old also debuted the music video for her new song Patient Zero - starring actors Colin Farrell and Dakota Johnson - during the Los Angeles ceremony, hosted by rapper Snoop Dogg.

The dark gothic thriller is her first music video since marrying NFL player Travis Kelce.

The song is one of four new tracks on The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore, which dropped last week.

In a ceremony that largely awarded female artists, Madonna went into the night with the most nominations - 13.

And her team also won best cinematography and choreography both for Confessions II, the film.

"Most of you were probably not born when I performed at the very first VMAs 43 years ago," the 68-year-old said after winning artist of the year.

She went on to recall how she had fallen over and exposed her backside, an accident which had threatened to end her fledgling career.

Reflecting on more recent times, she added: "I spent the last year and a half finding myself, believing in myself and really making the music that I wanted to make."

Madonna's opening performance - her first VMAs show since her infamous onstage kiss with Britney Spears in 2003 - included a live duet with Carpenter, and an appearance from British Brat star Charli XCX who features on her recent remix Danceteria (Afterhours).

While accepting the award for best collab, Madonna claimed Carpenter's team had originally kept her waiting.

"When five days passed and I still didn't get connected with Sabrina and didn't hear back from her about whether she wanted to do a song with me - five days - I DM'd [direct messaged] her," said the star.

"She answered me back and... within weeks we were in the studio together," she continued. "It was fabulous."

Carpenter, who grimaced slightly at the thought of her team having left the pop icon hanging, clarified: "My team replies. Just so everybody knows, they do respond to people.

"But I respond faster. So direct line to me is always the best way to get in contact."

British singers Raye and Sienna Spiro, who won best new artist, also performed on the night, where there were tributes to the late Parton and George Michael.

Another Brit, PinkPantheress won best art direction alongside Sweden's Zara Larsson for Stateside.

BTS picked up best group and song of the year for Swim, Olivia Rodrigo's The Cure won best alternative and Nirvana were honoured with the Video Vanguard award.

articles.title: ‘They’ll never bring us dowwwwwwwn!’ Wicked’s stars pick their favourite songs from the smash hit
articles.text:
Idina Menzel originated the role of Elphaba, the witch of the west who turns out not to be so wicked (but still very green). She won a Tony on Broadway, starred in the West End run and made a cheeky cameo in the recent film version

I’ll never forget the exhilaration I felt the first time I sang Defying Gravity in dress rehearsal. All the lights were as they should be. The smoke machine was blowing. The orchestra was playing. I was locked into my safety belt and I started to rise up over the theatre. To have that incredible moment and to see how the audience leapt to their feet – I felt so proud but I also just wanted to cry.

I was part of the developmental process of writing Wicked for four years and stood at a piano with [composer and lyricist] Stephen Schwartz many a time, being introduced to new ideas and songs – often written just the night before. He came to really understand my voice. Not just how high I could hit a note but where it sat emotionally. Originally, Defying Gravity didn’t go up an octave at the end. It stayed in this low place. So I asked Stephen if I could take it up an octave – the whole song is soaring, I said, and I have it in me to go up there: “Looook to the western skiiiiiiy!” I do take credit for that change.

The final note is actually easy for me. It’s like a release. There are other notes I find much harder. Singing notes on an “E” vowel is not easy: “Bring meeeee down”, that’s really tricky. I actually botched that note in my call-back audition. But instead of falling to pieces, I looked at the accompanist and said: “I’m going to do that again.” And then I just took all this angst and frustration at not being perfect and nailed it. Joe Mantello [director of Wicked on Broadway] always told me that’s how he knew I was going to be their witch – because I had this power and ferocity about me. That’s why, to this day, whenever young people ask me for advice, I always tell them not to fear their mistakes. Embrace those moments.

Zizi Strallen plays Glinda the Good in the current West End cast. She’s used to stepping into the shoes of iconic roles – and hinting at cracks that lie beneath a pristine surface – after a breakout performance as Mary Poppins

Whatever you’re going through in your life, Wicked somehow manages to hit a nerve. Everyone can relate to not feeling accepted for who they truly are or trying to figure out different parts of their personality. I’ve definitely gone through phases where I’ve made mistakes or said the wrong thing – so I channel all of that when I sing.

Thank Goodness shows the journey Glinda goes on throughout the whole show. It tells the audience that’s she’s struggling with the prospect of fame and recognition – and all the things that come with being Glinda the Good – but also wanting to stand up for her friend Elphaba and for what’s right. She’s getting everything she ever dreamed of but at what cost? That’s a beautiful arc for any actor to play: to start a song at one point and finish at an entirely different emotional one.

It’s wonderful to perform but very difficult to learn. The rhythms are really different to how you think they’re going to be. Stephen wrote it so that it’s sung exactly the way you would speak it, with little gaps here and there: “There’s a kind of a sort of – cost.” It’s similar to the way that Sondheim writes. It only really made sense to me when I sang it with the full orchestra and their rhythms accompanying me.

Dancing Through Life

Jordan Litz played Fiyero, the student who gets romantically entangled with Glinda and Elphaba, more than 1,700 times in the US. He makes his West End debut in the role

Dancing Through Life wasn’t always in the show. It was originally a song called Which Way Is the Party? The lyrics were a little sleazy: “Which way is the next keg of winkie beer?” It was all very frat boy and didn’t have nearly the same carefree attitude. You can hear they kept some stuff from the original number – the intro and the bridge – but the rest of the song is much more light and easy.

This was initially the hardest song for me to do because it’s the one that’s least like me. Growing up, I wasn’t the super-cool popular kid. I was 5ft 4in in my freshman year, singing soprano in my high-school choir and wearing oversized trainers. Finding the confidence to play Fiyero didn’t come naturally. It was always the song I got the most notes on during rehearsals for the Broadway run. More swagger! More confidence!

For the first year, performing it was a constant battle – trying to find that carefree confidence. And that struggle would show up in my dancing. My moves weren’t big enough or sharp enough. You’re surrounded by these incredible dancers and it’s very easy to shrink into yourself and not commit. It took a lot of support from people around me, convincing me that I have it inside myself. I was fighting against the person I envisioned myself to be, growing up, and who I actually am today. That’s probably why it’s become my favourite number: it feels like the song that I’ve learned the most from.

Musical supervisor Stephen Oremus conducted and helped to craft the Broadway premiere of Wicked

The Wizard and I was Stephen’s third try at a song in that spot in the show and it unlocked Elphaba’s journey. The first try felt very earnest and wide-eyed. It was a beautiful and heartfelt song called Making Good, about this young green girl who just wanted to do good things. But it wasn’t quite multi-layered enough. The second attempt was written after Idina was cast. It was a little bit more soaring and it suited Idina’s voice and personality more: it was the next step towards giving the number more of a sweeping grand gesture. Then in the third version, Stephen just hit it. He was able to combine everything good from the other takes and make it work. It’s an amazingly simple song but brilliantly written and executed.

The way we built the orchestrations, you can feel the excitement and anticipation of the character. The colours and flow of the song are relatively simple as Elphaba’s working out her thoughts and then it all shifts when she gets to that “unlimited” bridge. The orchestration gets dreamy and really expansive musically. Elphaba throws her arm out and allows herself to really feel for the first time. You’re seeing this very cerebral and intense girl start to get excited about the possibility of it all. It’s overwhelmingly beautiful to me.

The offers from Hollywood came flooding in after Gregory Maguire wrote his novel Wicked, a spin on L Frank Baum’s The Wizard of Oz. But it wasn’t until composer and lyricist Stephen Schwartz suggested setting it to song that an adaptation felt possible – and Wicked’s musical journey began

The final song between Elphaba and Glinda was one that I approached very cautiously. I knew it was going to be the heart of the show. If we got it right, we had our emotional ending. If we didn’t, it could undercut everything that had come before. So I phoned my collaborator, Winnie Holzman, and talked to her about this final meeting. What kind of things would they say to one another? At one point Winnie said: “They’ve had such an enormous impact on each other – they’ve changed each other for good.” “Stop right there,” I said. “You’ve just given me the title.”

I always knew what the song was going to feel like. I wanted something that was heartfelt and uncovered. Completely vulnerable. A lot of Glinda’s songs are about presenting a specific version of herself to the public. But I wanted this song to feel like a true expression from the heart. Then I started to think about the lyrics. My daughter Jessica was visiting at the time. She’d always had a deep friendship with a woman, Sarah, whom she first met when they were six or seven. So I sat down with Jess and I said: “Imagine you’re only going to see Sarah one last time. What would you say?” Jess started to talk about people coming into each other’s lives for a reason, about helping and hurting each other and about forgiveness. I wrote it all down and that was pretty much the entire first verse of For Good. I think that’s one of the reasons the song has such an impact – because people intuitively feel the truth of it.

articles.title: Digger review – Tom Cruise’s loudmouth oil tycoon goes hard in Alejandro G Iñárritu’s eco-satire
articles.text:
A new movie from the Oscar-winning Mexican director Alejandro González Iñárritu is always an event. So it’s disconcerting to discover that the event in question is the most disappointing film of the year: an exasperatingly shallow, laborious, self-congratulatory satire with a trick up its sleeve, featuring very good actors giving not very good performances. There are moments to enjoy in Tom Cruise’s boisterous leading turn, yes, but the film’s value resides chiefly in some dreamlike and disturbing images, distorted and bulging from the screen, conjured by cinematographer Emmanuel Lubezki and production designer Dennis Gassner.

An ageing, paunchy Texan oil tycoon called “Digger” Rockwell is seen fretfully getting up in the morning, cooing over his horrible old incontinent cat, taking urgent messages from underlings about a certain situation developing in his drilling station in the frozen Arctic. He is played by Tom Cruise with a wispy baldingness and various other prostheses, together with a good-ol’-boy twang and a Stetson borrowed from Slim Pickens’s bomb-riding army major in Kubrick’s Dr Strangelove. His prized possession is the battered old shovel his granddaddy used a century before, digging for black gold as a penniless young man in the lone star state. Digger likes to brandish this to make a point.

Digger’s – and the world’s – troubles come to a head when he is informed by his cringingly polite, querulous and terrified chief scientist Ganesh (Riz Ahmed) that the company’s irresponsible drilling practices, of which Ganesh has been warning Digger for quite some time, have caused a crisis: a vast ice floe, many times the size of Manhattan island, has broken away from the Arctic landmass and is now moving quickly towards the coast of Norway. Its imminent landfall is going to be like a nuclear attack.

Aggressively unrepentant to the very end, Digger gets himself invited to the White House’s crisis meeting, chaired by the gaunt and unwell President Compson, crankily played by John Goodman, with various military top brass and besuited politicians, including the vice-president, a very bland role on which Michael Stuhlbarg is wasted. Digger effectively takes over as de facto C-in-C, lambasting the president’s pusillanimous reluctance to take responsibility for a situation that his political subsidies and permissions have created. Meanwhile, back at Digger’s residence, Sandra Hüller has next to nothing to do as his half-sister, a role whose substance may well have been abandoned in the edit.

But wait. The film’s shrill, scratchy characterisations are partly explained by a sudden, unexpected plot development, yet this only creates a second narrative strand in which the performances are … well … merely inhibited and uninteresting. Cruise’s set piece moment is his toweringly contemptuous speech to a stylised megaparliament of UN nincompoops, all of them shouting and pointing and dressed in grey, in which Digger defiantly lacerates their hypocrisy in affecting to despise oil, while remaining utterly addicted to it for all their consumer conveniences. (Tactfully, Digger does not attack movie stars’ private planes.) He also angrily says that moving over to renewables, including nuclear, is simply not viable. Really? Yet Digger’s claim remains unchallenged, part of what we are perhaps supposed to admire, in spite of ourselves, about his realist sense of everyone else’s bad faith.

It is only when the film’s big storytelling sideways lurch happens, that you can see how our investment in the action is undermined; it is enclosed within inverted commas, an unearned and somehow anticlimactic high concept, a situation which is not itself fully dramatised or investigated but presented as a fait accompli twist. As with Adam McKay’s Don’t Look Up, there may be a tacit consensus, understandable at some level, that at least we have a big mainstream movie which is talking about the biggest issue of our time, and we have a duty to suspend critical objection. Digger certainly resonates with Donald Trump’s greedy urge to despoil the Arctic and everywhere else. Yet there is something glib and overblown here. This film finds itself in a postmodern hole. And what do you do when you’re in a hole?

articles.title: ‘Stern, sensuous, almost kissable lips’: why sculptures can have far more power when they’re broken
articles.text:
The nose of Cleopatra VII was supposed to have been so beautiful that it changed the course of history: if it had been shorter, French philosopher Blaise Pascal wrote, “the whole face of the earth would have changed”. A visit to the Palazzo Strozzi in Florence, however, will leave you convinced that Cleo’s conk was only the second most stunning feature to ever grace the face of an Egyptian pharaoh. Among the more than 80 objects on display at an exhibition that opened last week is an astonishingly lifelike sculpture showing off the lips of Akhenaten, from the 14th century BC: a seagull shape resting on a pillow of lush flesh, at once both stern and sensuous, almost uncomfortably kissable.

It was Thomas Aquinas who first came up with the theory that we perceive things to be beautiful when they are intact and whole, but the Akhenaten sculpture is so striking precisely because it has a major blemish. Like all the objects shown in Florence, it is only a fragment: a shard of polished limestone found in the dumps south of the Great Aten Temple in the city of el-Amarna, showing only the ruler’s nose and mouth.

“One of the unique qualities of fragments is that they focus your attention on details,” says CD Dickerson, an expert in Renaissance and baroque art. “You wouldn’t have considered the subtle way that the lip has been crisply carved in this stone if it had been part of a bigger statue with a bunch of other features. Fragments make you think about objects in a different way.”

Entitled Broken: The Power of Fragments, the show that Dickerson has co-curated for the Palazzo Strozzi and the National Gallery of Art in Washington DC, explores why people throughout history have gone to great lengths to damage or destroy carefully crafted sculptures and statues. But along the way, it raises an even more intriguing question: why it is that some works of art have a more powerful emotional pull in a broken state than when whole?

Many of the objects shown here speak of fault lines in history. There is a decapitated lifesize statue of a kneeling prior from Romainmôtier in Switzerland, likely beheaded during the iconoclastic frenzy of the Protestant Reformation. The dismembered left foot and right hand of King Louis XIV are all that remains of an equestrian monument to the French royal after the revolution rolled across Paris’s Place Vendôme and put up a guillotine instead. Modernist sculptor Adolfo Wildt’s bust of Mussolini was adorned with a simple bullet through the forehead after the fall of the fascist regime.

The vandals were following an age-old tradition, says co-curator Andrew Sears. “Across the ancient world it was a common practice during regime changes or religious transformations to destroy images of the previous one because it was believed that the images contained some kind of life force of the ruler.”

In some cases, these defaced sculptures would stay on as a deterrent. “They were made to be displayed in that way,” says Sears. A 19AD bust representing Germanicus, heir to Tiberius, had its nose expertly hacked off, upper earlobes cut and forehead adorned with a cross by Christians who protested against the deification of Roman emperors. The past, we are reassured, was a foreign country with cruel rituals.

Broken starts to get more surprising and interesting where it explores brokenness as more than a result of historical fractures. A section called Sculpting the Fragment opens with an intriguing dogū figurine from ancient Japan. Little is known about these small, fired-clay statuettes with bulging coffee-bean eyes other than that they have been found in pieces all over burial sites in Japan.

Current research indicates that the function of dogū figurines may have been akin to modern-day birthday pinatas: smashed to celebrate not just the end of the old but also the start of the new. “It’s very clear that the culture was to make these sculptures to intentionally break them, and for communities to share pieces with each other,” says Dickerson. “Our contemporary perception of ancient cultures being more violent is not always accurate.”

Dickerson and Sears’ rummage through the darker corners of museum storage rooms has yielded little evidence of Aquinas’s equation of breakage with ugliness. Often, the opposite held true. From the early 15th-century Aztec capital of Tenochtitlan, they present a statue of a reclining figure that was intentionally decapitated, as part of a campaign to rebuild a temple. Modelling their approach on the ruinous state of their surroundings, the Mexica seem to have understood completion to be unattainable. A broken artwork was proper because it revealed the true state of the world.

We may think of the cult of ruined buildings and broken statues as an obsession of the Romantics, of the paintings of Caspar David Friedrich or the “colossal wreck” of Percy Shelley’s Ozymandias. But Dickerson says ruin lust was already embedded in the art and literature of the Renaissance from the 13th century onwards. One of the most striking displays in Florence is a Michelangelo terracotta model of a headless and armless woman. Dated around 1533, it looks damaged but isn’t. Instead, it was the Renaissance’s answer to a pair of pre-distressed grunge-wash jeans: recent technical analysis of the torso’s breakage points suggests Michelangelo deliberately sculpted a fragment, in homage to the awe-inspiring antiquities that were being excavated in Rome at the time.

The exhibition culminates with contemporary artistic takes on broken sculptures, such as a Louise Bourgeois foot in a leg brace and German artist Julius von Bismarck’s collapsable equestrian statue of his chancellor forebear, Otto. If that feels slightly self-restraining, it’s because the wholeness v brokenness divide is still everywhere in modern popular culture once you start looking for it. Here the far-right social media accounts with immaculate classical busts as avatars, the impeccably smooth aesthetics of the iPhone, the flattened masks of the “clean girl” makeup trend; there the rise of broken bodies on the big screen, from Mad Max’s one-armed Furiosa to cleft-lipped lead actors like Tom Burke and Franz Rogowski and Game of Thrones’ “cripples, bastards and broken things”.

Clearly, the answer to the question of whether there is a beauty in brokenness is not just one that captured ancient civilisations, but continues to be one of the central cultural dividing lines of our time.

Broken: The Power of the Fragment is at Palazzo Strozzi, Florence, 25 September 2026 until 24 January, and at the National Gallery of Art, Washington, from 13 March to 27 June 2027
